items.title: We Took over ChatGPT Accounts
items.author: armcat
items.content:
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.

An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as with access to the victim's authenticated web session.

We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.

The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.

OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.

The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.

It started with a graph and a Preview

The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?

ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.

At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read , which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.

The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.

Browsers call the relevant API . It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.

That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.

MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.

The message that should not have worked

The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:

MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of , which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.

When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.

This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through do not automatically run.

The next step was an using , a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:

MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.

Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP

ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.

YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:

The response began like this:

Ending our callback with made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.

We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.

Turning a lab bug into one public link

So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.

We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.

However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.

The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:

    The resulting link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.

    We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.

    The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.

    At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.

    At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as , which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.

    The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:

    GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2

    This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.

    Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.

    We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.

    The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.

    Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.

    What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed

    The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.

    Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:

      The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.

      OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.

      The defensive lessons are fairly simple:

        This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.

        Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code.
        Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript.
        Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click.
        Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh.
        Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program.
        Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof.
        OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1.
        OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated.
        CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained.
        OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.

        The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.

        The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:

        Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:

        acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

        The parser and CSP transition. The operation could create an iframe, but a script inserted directly that way would remain inert. The unsandboxed caused a fresh HTML document parse and inherited the embedding ChatGPT origin. That document also inherited the effective CSP captured during testing, which blocked inline code but permitted in .

        The oEmbed response returned HTTP 200 with Content-Type: text/javascript; charset=UTF-8 and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff; no Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header was observed. Google rewrote angle brackets in the callback, so the payload used classic syntax instead of arrow functions. Ending the program with consumed the error object appended by the endpoint.

        For the private-conversation proof, the function was converted to source with , double quotes were converted to single quotes, and whitespace was collapsed. then encoded it into the callback, the script URL was HTML-escaped inside , and that entire element was escaped again into the iframe's attribute. The final callback was 5,533 characters; the YouTube URL was 7,309 characters; the script element was 7,337 characters; and the final iframe markup was 7,390 characters.

        The same-origin frame parsed from the parent document, extracted the session access token and account ID, and required the account ID in the token to agree with the session when both were present. It used these in-memory headers:

        Authorization: Bearer <victim token>
ChatGPT-Account-ID: <victim account>
Accept: application/json

        The primary requests were:

        GET /backend-api/conversations?exclude_conversation_origin=tpp&expand=false&is_archived=false&is_starred=false&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<id>?num_turns=2&include_has_versions=true

        Only a 403, 404, or 405 on the detail request caused the code to try the legacy /backend-api/conversation/<id>?include_full_conversation=true route. The validation transmitted only a small selected value from the response. Before the external image request, it cleared references to the token, account, bootstrap, session, and request headers.

          The broader lesson is that security boundaries have to hold across the complete product, not just inside individual components. Any public or shareable surface should be treated as attacker-controlled input, every cross-frame message should be authenticated, and untrusted markup should remain sandboxed throughout its entire rendering path.

items.title: Switch Lowering in GCC
items.author: signa11
items.content:
We have seen in a previous post that switch statements are more complex than they seem. The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't). Is that everything it can do?

In this post, I'll focus on . All optimizations, except the bitset lowering, translate to clang. I'll be using the optimization flag unless indicated otherwise.

I've also slightly edited code and removed certain assertions for brevity.

Let us start with a simple example. A function that takes two integers and . Depending on the value of , it calls a corresponding function (, , and so forth) with as an argument and returns the result. Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

The compiler agrees with this approach, and transforms the switch statement into a jump table.

Moreover, it is able to identify when the values are offset by a constant:

Our intuition suggests that the more sparse the values, the less advantageous the jump table conversion is.

Through experimentation, we find that considers the threshold to be around eight jump table entries per label.

In other words, the following function compiles to a jump table:

But this other function is expanded as a tree of comparisons:

Here's the comparison tree visualized for clarity:

A couple of observations:

  1. We've only tried equally spaced values so far. Can the compiler identify transformations that are profitable on a subset of all cases?
  2. So far each led to a different result. What if we had different cases with the same result?
  3. The switch in could be simplified by dividing by eight before the jump. Interestingly, find this simplification.

Altering our first example by including an outlier value shows that the compiler is able to recognize dense subsets of cases.

The compiler emits a branch for case 100, but emits a jump table for case 1 through 5.

In our examples so far, each case statement lead to a different code block. Let's test what happens when multiple labels invoke the same function.

We have 20 case labels, with values between 0 and 87. The compiler could lower this to a jump table with 88 entries. Our hypothesis for the heuristic is that a jump table conversion is profitable when its size is smaller than . Since , the conversion should be profitable in this case, however opted to lower the switch to a sequence of comparisons.

To better understand why, let's examine a specific block of labels.

The compiler realizes that the cases are contiguous and can be implemented with two comparisons instead of four. If the input of the jump table heuristic is the number of instead of , things work out:

We have a total of 10 comparisons. Since , our revised heuristic suggests that a jump table transformation is unprofitable.

Let us try a non-contiguous case.

The compiler emits non-intuitive machine code. Why is there no nor jump tables? Where does the constant come from?

An hint comes from the instruction . According to the Intel docs, :

Selects the bit in a bit string (specified with the first operand, called the bit base) at the bit-position designated by the bit offset (specified by the second operand) and stores the value of the bit in the CF flag.

If we examine the binary representation of , we find that it is in fact a bitset. The bits that are set to one correspond to the ASCII values of the case labels, each value being reduced by 48.

We've encountered several distinct lowering strategies employed by gcc. For a more in-depth understanding, we can delve into the compiler's source code.

The compiler pass that responsible for lowering statements is the (appropriately named) , which in turn calls .

Since source can be daunting to follow, I'll provide a step-by-step commented version below. Following this, I will break down each section to explain its functionality.

Some preamble code. points to a gimple object. Gimple is the internal representation used by . Through this, we extract the overall count of cases and the individual counts of cases for each outgoing edge.

We also allocate a vector that will record the lowering strategy chosen for each case label.

More setup code. We notice that gimple has a concept of high and low value for each label. That is, contiguous labels have already joined together at this stage.

For each case label, we allocate a . This cluster serves as a record, capturing the range of values associated with the label, the relevant output edge, and the likelihood of this cluster being chosen. This probability comes from profile-guided optimization. By default it is uniform among case labels.

We transform the vector of clusters we have created. The name hints to the bitset lowering strategy we saw before.

This section allocates a vector for the transformed cases and a scratch vector. Any case that wasn't altered during the bitset transformation process is gathered in this scratch vector. These cases are then processed and cleared whenever we come across an optimized cluster.

Essentially, in this section we are looking for sequences of case labels that couldn't be converted into bitset clusters.

We attempt to convert these consecutive labels into a jump table and add the outcome to the output.

This is a coda for the loop above.

Whatever is left goes through another pass, which turns the switch statement into a decision tree. The bitsets and jump table are leaves of the decision tree.

Let's dig further into bit_test_cluster::find_bit_tests. The high level structure of the code is as follow.

Initially, we aim to find the optimal method to bundle all clusters into bitsets. Optimality, in this context, refers to minimizing the number of bitsets used. We do so using dynamic programming.

Subsequently, we iterate over the bitsets and apply a profitability heuristic. If the bitsets meet this heuristic, we emit a ; otherwise, we keep the original s.

For the dynamic programming, we'll use a vector of structures. Each has three components:

  • The first records how many bitsets do we need to represent the first case labels, where is the index in the vector.
  • The second records the of the last bitset.

The dynamic programming is as follows. We want to find the minimum number of bitsets to represent the first case labels.

The base case is straightforward, a single case label can be represented by a single bitset.

Suppose we have already have found the optimal number of bitsets for the first case label, for all . We define to be the optimal number of splits for the first elements. This means we already computed , and are now seeking .

If the range of case labels can be represented as a bitset cluster, it must be true that

Conversely, assume we have the optimal assignment for the first labels. If the last bitset starts at label , this assignment is also optimal when restricted to . Were this not the case, we could improve the assignment on as well.

Therefore, it must be that:

These conditions are exactly what the statement in the code above checks for.

The function controls whether a range of labels can be turned into a bitset test. It tests two criteria:

  • The range of all the case labels must be smaller than the width of a register. On contemporary systems, the combined range should be less than 64.
  • The case labels must have at most 3 outgoing edges.

If there is more than one edge, we emit a cascade of bit tests.

Now we convert only bitsets that satisfy the test. In the code represents the number of case labels handled by the cluster, while denotes the number of distinct outgoing edges.

The logic for jump table conversion mirrors the one used for bit test conversion. It leverages dynamic programming to identify "clusters" that can be profitably converted to a jump table.

Let's delve into the code.

We start by preallocating a vector of . We'll use this vector to keep track of the best jump table assignments for consecutive clusters.

We also push the base case for dynamic programming. This corresponds to using a single jump table for the whole .

Let's focus now on the main loop.

The dynamic programming loop mirrors the one we used for bitsets. We want to find the minimum number of jump tables to represent the first i case labels.

We iterate over splits at the -th case label, for . During each iteration we track the best scoring split. The special case represents a single jump table for the entire statement.

Inside this inner loop we also keep track of:

  1. How many distinct jump tables we would need to lower the switch.
  2. The of the jump table of the decomposition.
  3. How many cases be handled by a jump table. In the code, this is the accumulator .

Point 1. and 2. are analogous to the bitset lowering pass, while 3. is new and specific to jump tables.

Namely, there is some overhead to dispatching to a jump table, due to the indirect jump and the need to check bounds. Therefore requires a minimum amount of labels to generate a jump table.

If a split would generate a jump table that is too small, the size of the jump table is added to an accumulator , which is used as a tie-breaker between different split candidates.

To compute the scoring, we need the comparison count between -th and the -th case label. We compute it summing up the number of comparisons for all labels, and decreasing the count as we progress in the inner loop.

We also need the number of unhandled labels. We determine it comparing the size of the jump table to the result of the function. This function is architecture dependent and takes into account the presence of switch-case specific instructions, but on modern x64 and Arm64 machines, it defaults to 5.

Let's now focus on the main heuristic, starting with how is computed. I've reproduced below the main loop, omitting lines unrelated to the main heuristic.

We've seen in the examples section that gcc uses the ratio between jump table entries and comparisons as a metric for the lowering the heuristic. The code below shows that distinct ratios are used when optimizing for speed (flags ) or size (flag ). Specifically, a ratio of 8 is used when optimizing for speed, while a ratio of 2 is used when optimizing for size.

Now onto the main loop. Given two splits, we prefer the one that results in fewer jump tables being emitted. Or, if they would result in the same number of jump tables, we prefer the one that handles the most labels. We also ignore splits that would result in unprofitable jump tables, where profitability is checked by the function.

The condition, checks for overflow and compares the ratio of case labels to jump table entries:

The coda of the function also mirrors the one for bitset clusters. It iterates over all jump tables in reverse order, and prunes the ones that fail the check.

The check for jump tables aims to prune small jump tables. It compares the number of case labels to .

If cannot emit a bitset cluster or a jump table, it falls back to a binary tree of comparison.

In emitting the tree, it takes into account the probability of each case label cluster. The probability can be obtained via profile-guided optimization, or with the __builtin_expect_with_probability builtin.

The code is pretty straightforward.

Sum probability of all case labels.

Split the case label list such that both halves have equal probability.

Recurse in both halves to build the binary tree.

We've seen the heuristics and lowering strategies employs when compiling switch statements, including:

  • Compressing multiple labels into a bitset.
  • Transforming the statement into a jump table.
  • Transforming the statement into a binary decision tree.

Finally, I want to thank B.X.V., C.P., and V.P. for their feedback when writing this post

Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026:

Subject: Notice of Security Incident

This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.

We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.

We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).

We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.

We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.

Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:

    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.
For more information

We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.

The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.

What Scribd, Inc. is doing

    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.
We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.

items.title: Sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust
items.author: wh33zle
items.content:
Today, we are announcing : a sans-IO Rust implementation of the WireGuard® state machine, optimized for ease of use, security and performance through a parallel-friendly and idiomatic API.

sans-IO is the idea that you design your system such that IO and side-effects are cleanly separated from the state and "business logic". The IO in sans-IO doesn't just mean file or network IO. It also includes things like time and randomness!

Due to their lack of side-effects, sans-IO components compose very well and are relatively easy to test. The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules.

The code examples and references in this post are in Rust but sans-IO isn't Rust-specific at all. Its patterns and ideas can be applied in any language. For a more in-depth explanation, our sans-IO post is a good place to start.

When we first built Firezone, we reached for as our WireGuard implementation. more or less did what we wanted, but over time, we found ourselves patching our fork over and over with bug fixes as well as API additions. The goal was to allow these patches to still be upstreamed, so we always kept the existing API working the way it was.

What we found was that retaining 100% API compatibility with upstream was increasingly difficult as our product requirements evolved. One of the first big changes we made to was to make it fully sans-IO with regard to time handling (firezone/boringtun#5). This meant adding new APIs for everything with a suffix that would take an . sans-IO time handling is very important if you want to accurately simulate an entire system. See this blog post to learn more about how we do that.

Another thing we feature-flagged was internal buffering. At first, it seems convenient that establishes a session automatically if you don't have one yet (or anymore) and you are trying to send a packet. Internal buffering, however, comes with several problems:

  1. At some point, the buffer needs to be drained. solves this by requiring you to call with a zero-length datagram. Rather unintuitive.
  2. It incurs additional allocations (at least in the way it was implemented in ).
  3. Buffer sizes should be configurable / tunable.

All of these problems point at the same solution: Just don't buffer in the library. It simplifies the interface and the implementation on both sides.

The full list of patches and fixes is pretty long. Even excluding dependency bumps, that is more than 70 PRs. Several of them are fixes for edge-cases we discovered. Others add new APIs or make certain aspects configurable.

After more than 2 years of using and patching , we had a pretty good idea of what the overall API of a userspace WireGuard implementation should be. Now it exists as .

The core building blocks of the sans-IO API are now:

  • Handling inbound packets:
    • Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation
    • Tunnel::handle_handshake_response
    • Tunnel::handle_cookie_reply
    • Tunnel::begin_decapsulate & Tunnel::commit_decapsulate
  • Handling outbound packets: Tunnel::begin_encapsulate
  • Handling timer updates: &
  • Handling events:

Without internal buffering, there is no API contract that requires you to call certain APIs in a loop, which fits much better into the overall sans-IO model. To send a packet, you call Tunnel::begin_encapsulate. It is up to you to buffer the packet if you don't have a session yet. Creating a new session means sending a handshake. You can initiate a new handshake at any point with Tunnel::initiate_handshake.

The design of these APIs is very deliberate and will make more sense if we quickly recap the WireGuard protocol.

WireGuard's message format supports 4 types of messages: handshake init, handshake response, cookie reply and encrypted data.

Every WireGuard session starts with a Diffie-Hellman key exchange which is a moderately expensive operation. WireGuard's design ensures that exposing an endpoint doesn't open up a DoS opportunity.

Anyone who knows the endpoint's public key can easily create bogus handshake initiations and forge the source IP of the incoming UDP packet. The receiving WireGuard implementation has to run its half of the DH operations before it can tell that the supplied handshake data is bogus. But at that point, the CPU resources have already been spent. Send enough handshake initiations and the receiving end will spend all its CPU cycles on handling irrelevant handshakes.

To prevent this, WireGuard specifies a cookie mechanism that forces the remote to prove ownership of its claimed source IP, which in turn allows rate-limiting handshakes per source IP.

These rate limits apply to an entire WireGuard interface and not just to a single tunnel.

Once a handshake has been completed, both peers can exchange encrypted data packets with a symmetric cipher. As part of the handshake, the peers also exchange their locally-chosen session indices. These indices enable de-multiplexing of tunnels as well as multiple sessions within a tunnel.

If you are working in a language like Rust, chances are you enjoy using types. And using types well means enforcing invariants at compile-time such that you can't even ship a certain bug in the first place. For example, forgetting to apply the rate limiter to a message would be pretty bad because it doesn't show up under normal operation. Similarly, routing an incoming packet to the wrong tunnel is something that will only show up in production.

A good API design makes it impossible to build things that are broken and also guides you along in understanding how the protocol works.

A WireGuard interface is identified by a single key and a tunnel is a connection between two interfaces. Any time we want to send a packet, we therefore need to specify which tunnel it should be sent on and when we receive a packet, we need to figure out which tunnel it belongs to.

In , these concepts directly map to the and types. All inbound packets go through . That is the only public API that parses a raw datagram. It parses the packet, applies rate limits and hands you back a with one enum variant per WireGuard message type, or a cookie reply to send back if the interface is under load. These then map directly to the corresponding functions on a : Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation, etc. Handshake initiations are routed by the initiator's static public key. All other messages expose they should be dispatched to, identified by a .

Under the hood, does a lot of things for you here. It parses the tunnel index and extracts the upper 24 bits, it applies rate limits, generates cookie replies and validates handshake messages.

Crucially, the constructors for types like are all crate-private. Even though exposes a public handle_handshake_initiation function, the only way to call that is by going through first to obtain such a type. And protects your application by applying the rate limiter, all without you having to think about it.

One of the best features of is its parallel-friendly API for encrypting and decrypting packets.

On a protocol level, WireGuard doesn't share any state between tunnels. Therefore, parallelizing a WireGuard implementation across peers is very easy.

But what about parallelizing work within a single tunnel? WireGuard operates on layer 3, and thus a single session with another peer carries the traffic of many individual network flows. Even if we handle tunnels to different peers on different threads, all network flows (i.e., unique 5-tuples) toward the same host or subnet will be processed sequentially, effectively bounded by how fast the CPU is at ChaCha20-Poly1305, WireGuard's cipher for data packets. To protect against replay by malicious on-path observers, WireGuard data packets have a monotonically increasing packet counter. This counter is scoped to a single session and therefore would require synchronization if we were to access this state from multiple threads simultaneously.

To avoid this, separates the bookkeeping from the actual encryption and decryption. Calling Tunnel::begin_encapsulate doesn't in fact encrypt anything. It checks for the current session, reserves a packet counter, advances timer state and then hands you a :

 {
    <>(, plaintext: &[], dst: & []) <DataMessage<>, Error> {
        
    }
}

implements and can thus be transferred to another thread to perform the bulk of the work. Running in the repository showcases the effect of this split:

data_path/64B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/64B/encrypt   time:   [226.15 ns 226.22 ns 226.29 ns]
data_path/64B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.600 ns 37.675 ns 37.744 ns]
data_path/64B/decrypt   time:   [205.78 ns 205.83 ns 205.87 ns]
data_path/64B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.486 ns 17.529 ns 17.575 ns]

data_path/1280B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/1280B/encrypt time:   [933.49 ns 933.54 ns 933.59 ns]
data_path/1280B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.606 ns 37.681 ns 37.751 ns]
data_path/1280B/decrypt time:   [914.81 ns 914.89 ns 914.97 ns]
data_path/1280B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.657 ns 17.707 ns 17.764 ns]

As expected, the bookkeeping parts (, and ) do not scale with packet size. What does scale with packet size are the and functions. At a packet size of 1280 bytes, the bookkeeping part of encrypting a new packet is only 2%. If we move the actual encryption to another thread, this hints at a potential speedup of more than 45x!

An effective speedup of 45x is hard to achieve in practice because it ignores the cost of passing to another thread and assumes no other overhead is introduced. Nevertheless, being able to offload the crypto to worker threads allows for some great throughput improvements.

Being a sans-IO library, doesn't concern itself with how exactly you want to parallelize your crypto. If you want to keep it simple, you can also just call and inline and not bother with parallelization at all.

The key thing we wanted to achieve with 's API design was to enable parallel crypto while keeping everything around single-threaded. This lets the internal rate limiter work without locks or atomic counters and take advantage of Rust's borrow checker, all while combining state from multiple tunnels.

With , our fork at is now deprecated. If you are building on top of WireGuard, whether that's a VPN, a mesh network or something else entirely, we hope makes your life a little easier. It is available on crates.io.

items.title: AO3 Down for Maintenance
items.author: idlewords
items.content:
Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far. However, we want to make some things clear:

First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe.

Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password.

We use industry-standard techniques for storing passwords in a scrambled form that cannot easily be reversed. Even so, no hashing method can fully protect a weak or reused password from being cracked. As a precaution, we recommend that you change your passwords on any other sites where you use the same password as on AO3.

AO3 does not collect real names, so none could be exposed. Additionally, our donor information is held in an entirely separate system and is never linked to AO3, so that data has also not been exposed.

We will update everyone as our investigation continues; we may be unable to respond to individual inquiries from users. Please keep an eye on our official outlets for updates. Our next update will be posted when we have further information available.

Our current expectation is that AO3 will be down for a minimum of two weeks; however, it could take up to four weeks. During that time, we may be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state, meaning that not all features will be available and/or the site may be read-only. If we are able to do that, please be aware that we might have to bring the site back down unexpectedly as part of our recovery efforts. We will keep you in the loop for any developments.

items.title: Jules Verne's Lost Novel
items.author: dnetesn
items.content: In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. Hetzel thought the prophecy implausible and the tone too bleak. Verne put the manuscript away. It remained unpublished for 131 years, until it was recovered from a family safe and finally appeared in France in 1994. We commonly describe Verne as a great…

items.title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
items.author: dxs
items.content:
For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.

Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.

But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.

And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.

One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.

By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.

The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.

“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.

He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.

The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.

But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.

Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.

“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.

Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.

“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:

“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."

Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.

“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.

'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'

Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.

So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.

Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.

items.title: Infinite Mac: BeOS
items.author: ecliptik
items.content:
You can now run many BeOS versions in the browser at Infinite Mac, my site where you can experience the Macintosh Cinematic Universe from 1984 to 2005. The installs are full peers to their Mac cousins: you can boot them instantly (large disks are streamed in), play around with pre-installed software from Infinite HD, insert CD-ROMs from the Internet Archive, and save your work on the “Saved HD” drive.

BeOS was a multimedia-focused, multi-tasking and multi-threaded OS that was eventually ported to the Power Macintoshes of the mid-90s. It impressed many in the Mac community, including Apple itself, who considered acquiring Be, the company that had created it. If you’ve been following the saga of Apple’s search for a next-generation operating system, this lets you see what the road not taken was like.

After the last somewhat involved (though still satisfying) project on Infinite Mac, I was looking for a quicker win. BeOS had been on my radar for a while, and (unlike A/UX) I had a personal connection to it: I remember spotting a BeBox in Akihabara, making my Mac cosplay as it with BeView, and eventually dual-booting BeOS on my Power Macintosh 8500. DingusPPC, an emulator I had already integrated, was making good progress on running BeOS, so it seemed like adding it to the site would be mostly a matter of preparing some additional disk images.

Initially it appeared to be as straightforward as I had hoped; I added a Power Macintosh 7300 configuration (one of the Power Macs that was officially supported), found an install CD, made a disk image, and was up and running. But as I used it more and started to install additional versions, I began to find a lot of small bugs and edge cases:

  • The BeOS boot loader thought that all modifier keys were being held down due to a bug in the ADB emulation; this made it present the (ugly, PC BIOS-like) partition choice screen every time.
  • When changing the screen depth, there are two hardware components that need to be notified: the video controller and the digital-to-analog converter. DingusPPC had been accidentally relying on the order that Mac OS sent these notifications in; BeOS happened to make the opposite choice and would end up with a corrupted display.
  • Early versions of BeOS did video memory updates in little-endian mode; DingusPPC was missing support for that hardware capability.
  • Later versions of BeOS could mount HFS partitions, but they were having trouble with the volumes that I generated via the Python library. It turned out that BeOS was (correctly) stricter than Mac OS about how some data structures should be populated.

SheepShaver, a Power Macintosh emulator that is still around today (and that Infinite Mac also embeds), originated on BeOS. Mostly for the fun of another layer of inception/emulation, I wanted to make sure that it worked too. As it turned out, it also required a compatibility fix – it relied on an edge case of how the ROM is mapped to physical memory addresses that DingusPPC did not accurately model.

There is a pattern to most of these bug fixes: DingusPPC (and Infinite Mac) have been mostly focused on running Mac OS, and thus accidentally became dependent on its quirks or implementation choices. Adding an independently developed operating system to the mix exercised new paths, and ended up improving the accuracy of the emulated hardware. To be clear, DingusPPC was pretty close out of the box; kudos to itsmaintainers. I believe that, with this work, it’s the only emulator that can run PowerPC versions of BeOS. I’m also hopeful that this will help with bringing up alternate operating systems like MkLinux (which I also have memories of) and Rhapsody.

On the Infinite Mac side, there were obvious changes like a “BeOS” appearance for my custom controls and collecting software for the library. I also needed to overlay some dynamically generated content on the disk to get the OS to preselect a screen resolution that matches the browser window’s (similar to what was done for A/UX). An AI agent (still Codex for me) was once again helpful for this type of fiddly reverse-engineering task: it’s one thing to observe that the OS stores a file on disk with the screen size; it’s another to be able to reproduce all its nuances, especially as the format changed with later releases.

Developer Release 8.2, the initial BeOS version for Power Macs, had a time bomb that kept it from booting after April 1, 1997. This was not just to create a sense of urgency; it shipped with a licensed font renderer that Be could not distribute indefinitely. DR8.3 addressed this, but to make that notable first version bootable, I did end up relying on the custom date support to hardcode a working date when choosing that disk.

Though I did kick the tires of BeOS back when it was current, I don’t recall using it enough to form any opinions beyond “this is fast; I miss all my third-party software.” About This Particular Macintosh does have contemporary coverage, including Be’s first and second appearances at Macworld Expo Boston, and reviews of R3 and R4.5; they make for interesting reading. This video released by Be itself also has a walkthrough of what they considered its strengths.

Looking at it with 2026 eyes, I am still struck by its speed – it’s fast to boot and to use, especially when compared with its contemporary Mac OS releases that do so much less (e.g. live window dragging did not appear until Mac OS X). The POSIX subsystem and the Unix-like shell also feel modern (unlike A/UX’s) – I had no trouble using the terminal to poke around. There’s also plenty of innovation, though some of it (BFS with its attributes and live queries) is more interesting than the rest (replicants are a precursor to widgets, but I couldn’t think of a use for them).

It also feels like a developer-focused and under-construction system: many of the included apps are technology demos (though who doesn’t love a Utah teapot), while a contemporary Be homepage links directly to the developer release notes and discusses CodeWarrior releases and access to the bug tracker. The unfinished nature extends to third-party software too – I stumbled across some BeOS software on this Amiga magazine CD, and most of it had a “version 0.1” feel, either literally or figuratively. To be fair, I did find some more fleshed-out software, for example, Gobe Productive from the former ClarisWorks team. This and other software is on Infinite HD if you’d like to try it out (preferably in later OS versions).

The interface seemed novel at the time, though I wonder how it would have held up. The distinctive tabbed window titles look neat, but they have a reduced draggable area, so I’d have to think harder every time I wanted to move a window. And using a hand as the default cursor makes clicking feel less precise than a traditional arrow (just which of the pixels on the “finger” is the hotspot?). Other parts of the UI feel like a not-fully-coherent Windows/Mac hybrid, with a Deskbar that can emulate a Start menu, Alt key accelerators on menu items, but also spring-loaded folders and a spatial Tracker.

Speaking of the Tracker, I had not realized that Be had open-sourced it (and even incorporated changes from the open-source version). This was around the time that Be pivoted away to internet appliances – there’s no need to invest engineering resources in a file manager if all that’s exposed is one full-screen browser app. This interview with the Tracker developer has more of the backstory.

NeXTStep, by comparison, feels more mature. It had gone through some similar churn (proprietary hardware to off-the-shelf PCs, company strategy shifts), but, perhaps because it had more time, it handled things a bit more gracefully. For example, NeXT supported “fat” binaries that could run on 68K, Intel, PA-RISC and other architectures. On BeOS they had to be separate executables, making the user choose which to run and complicating distribution (this made it harder for me to find software to include in Infinite HD). Worse yet, you also had to have parallel disk partitions on CD-ROMs: BFS used the host endianness, so disks written by a PowerPC install could not be read by an Intel one, or vice versa. But my pro-NeXT bias may be due to knowing which OS Apple ended up picking.

It’s only been a short while since the last update, but I did squeeze in a couple of quality-of-life improvements. You can now take screenshots and record videos (with sound) of the emulated machine’s screen. This gives you a high-fidelity way to capture image content, since it’s a direct dump of what would have been shown on the screen.

I also expanded the collection of operating system CD-ROMs with items like the Rhapsody and Mac OS X developer previews. While they’re aspirational for now (DingusPPC can’t run them yet), they do satisfy my completionist tendencies. These CDs are mirrored to and served from my own Cloudflare R2 bucket – the Internet Archive is an incredible resource (you can donate to them), but streaming from it has been increasingly flaky. I don’t want to add to the problem, and thanks to my sponsors, I can afford to serve a few gigabytes.

As for what’s next, with this alternate Mac timeline covered, it may be time to explore a prequel.

items.title: Bunny CDN Security Incident
items.author: SondreDag
items.content:
We're reaching out to inform you of a security incident involving one of our infrastructure providers, the steps we've taken, and what this means for you.

- What happened and how we responded

Last week, one of our infrastructure providers reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software. One of our CDN nodes, located in Armenia, was hosted on a server supplied by this provider.

After receiving the alert from the affected provider, our engineering team took immediate action. Within 20 minutes, we stopped routing traffic through the server. We then reviewed and preserved the relevant security logs for investigation, securely wiped the server, and revoked its access to our other systems. The affected server has been permanently removed from our infrastructure.

Our investigation found no evidence of unauthorized access to the CDN node or any of its data. The infrastructure provider has also found no evidence that our server was accessed, but continues to investigate the incident.

- What this means for your data

While neither investigation has found any indication of unauthorized access to our server, we cannot completely rule out the possibility.

If unauthorized access to our CDN node did occur, the potentially exposed information would have been: temporarily cached CDN content, Pull Zone configurations, and TLS certificates stored on that server.

As an additional precaution, we have revoked and reissued all TLS certificates for bunny.﻿net platform domains (b-cdn.﻿net and bunny.﻿run). Reissuance of managed TLS certificates for custom domains is ongoing and is expected to be completed within the next 24 hours. No action is required from customers using managed certificates. We will post a further update on our status page once this process is complete.

If you manage your own TLS certificates, we recommend revoking and reissuing them with new private keys as a precaution.

No other customer data, including bunny.﻿net account data, was stored on the server in question, and no internal systems were affected.

We’re closely monitoring our infrastructure and working with the affected provider as the investigation continues. Should any new findings affect our customers, we will provide an update via email and on our status page.

At bunny.﻿net, we understand the trust you place in us to keep your content secure, and we take that responsibility seriously. If you have any questions or need help with managing your TLS certificates, our support team will be happy to assist.

items.title: US tech stocks see sharp falls over AI cost fears
items.author: mindracer
items.content:
Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).

Shares in Intel plummeted by 28% on Friday, while Google owner Alphabet saw its stock price continue to fall another 1.4% after a 12% plunge on Thursday.

Other tech stocks, including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, ended October with its worst monthly slide since March 2025.

While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.

Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800bn between them in 2026.

At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.

The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere however, with Intel shedding more than $130bn in value.

The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.

On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.

"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.

In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.

items.title: AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them
items.author: dorianniemiec
items.content:
There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.

Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?

Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.

Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).

Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.

Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.

Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.

Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.

Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.

Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.

PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.

  • Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.

  • Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.

  • Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.

This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.

recent study

research

you don’t feel it happening

For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.

SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.

We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.

A few approaches worth considering:

human-practice opportunities

Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side.

Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.

Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.

Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.

One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.

And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.

items.title: The federated code forge
items.author: zlliang
items.content:
For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.

But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.

Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.

It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.

Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.

Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agentfriendly.

The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become .

The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.

Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.

This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.

The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.

The new data model and repo-owned data

First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under , replacing the old records.

Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.

With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.

In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.

But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.

If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!

Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.

Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.

This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.

Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.

items.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
items.author: paulpauper
items.content:
FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa.

A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.

The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.

The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

items.title: Medicare Will Pay $50k for Your Heart Attack. It Should Pay $100 to Prevent It
items.author: brandonb
items.content:
We are currently in a "golden age of medical science," yet in a "dark age of healthcare delivery." An important illustration is the diagnosis and treatment of America's number one cause of death and disability, coronary artery disease. More than 800,000 Americans suffer a heart attack each year. The great majority of these events are preventable. The coronary artery calcium score (CAC) is a simple 10-minute scan that can identify the presence and amount of coronary atherosclerosis many years before it causes a heart attack. It costs about $100 and uses a fraction of the radiation of a standard chest CT.

In March 2026, after more than three decades of accumulated evidence, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) finally gave CAC a central role in their national guidelines for the prevention of coronary artery disease. The CAC scan, which detects calcified plaque in the arteries, is recommended for adults with borderline or intermediate risk of coronary disease for whom the decision to start preventive therapy such as statin drugs remains uncertain.

For decades, doctors have relied on risk calculators built around age, sex, serum cholesterol, diabetes status, blood pressure, and smoking to estimate who might have a heart attack. The calculators estimate probability, not the actual presence of coronary atherosclerosis. In contrast, a CAC scan detects the disease itself. This is important because a patient with a borderline or low cholesterol may already have extensive plaque, while another with a high cholesterol may have none. A calcium score of zero re-classifies risk downward and thereby can avoid unnecessary pharmacologic treatment, such as statins. A score above 100 identifies patients who may benefit from pharmacologic and aggressive lifestyle intervention.

An excellent illustration of the role of CAC scanning is Rob*, a 52-year-old patient we saw recently. He exercises regularly, eats well, and has borderline high cholesterol. He has a family history of heart disease but no other known cardiac risk factors. The standard risk calculator places him in a low risk category, and he would prefer to defer treatment.

His CAC score, however, tells a different story. It is 220, indicating a substantial atherosclerotic plaque burden for a man his age. Genetics account for roughly half of cardiovascular risk, but the risk calculators do not include genetics. The scan demonstrated that drug treatment gives Rob his best chance of preventing a future heart attack.

Despite mountains of evidence proving its superiority over conventional risk factors for predicting heart attacks, CAC scanning has been included only peripherally in national guidelines for the past 35 years. Why?

Part of the delay is structural. Clinical decision support tools were built to modify population-average risk factors, not to incorporate individualized imaging. Guideline committees move cautiously, as they should, and prevention is harder to standardize than intervention. Cardiologists and primary care doctors, constrained by what insurers will cover, are left offering the test mainly to patients who can pay cash out of pocket.

With the updated ACC/AHA guideline, heart attack prevention is finally aligning around a simple principle: when possible, measure the disease.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is also changing the economics of prevention. Millions of Americans already undergo chest CT scans for other reasons, yet the cardiovascular information visible on those scans is often ignored. AI can identify coronary and vascular calcification opportunistically, standardize reporting, and flag patients who should receive formal preventive evaluation. That's especially important for patients least able to pay cash for elective testing.

AI-CAC is now being used to measure soft plaque, an important precursor to hard plaque seen on traditional calcium scores. Used responsibly, AI-enabled CAC analysis could help move heart disease prevention to the population health level.

Heart attacks are largely preventable, and we have had the means to find the disease and treat it in time for more than a generation. What we have lacked is a payment system that spends $100 to avoid a $50,000 emergency.

The story of CAC isn't so unique. It is the story of how a low-cost, low-risk, well-studied tool can sit at the edge of clinical practice for decades because the systems around it -- the guidelines, the reimbursement codes, the habits of practice -- were not built to absorb it.

The evidence has been strong for years, and the guidelines have finally caught up.

*Patient's name changed for confidentiality.
