items.title: The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes
items.author: domhudson
items.content:
investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

items.title: How do you take a picture of a black hole?
items.author: dverlaeckt80
items.content:
Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?

Okay. I’m Janna Levin

And I’m Steve Strogatz.

And this is

A podcast from where we look at some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.

Welcome to another episode.

Great to see you.

Great to see you. I’m pretty excited about this one. I cannot deny or hide it. We’re talking about not only an area where I’ve spent a lot of my life black holes — the greatest, strangest topic out there — but also I had a chance to talk to an old friend. So it’s a fun episode, I hope.

I’m really looking forward to hearing it. I know you’ve always had a special affection for black holes. I’ve had a chance to interview you in some earlier version of this.

And you blew my mind over and over about black holes.

Yeah, they require some defense. They’ve got a bad reputation, not entirely earned.

What’s the bad reputation? Because they like to eat things?

Yeah. You know, black holes, kind of this monster truck language around black holes all the time. You know, they’re like… But actually, black holes are remarkably elegant, clean, simple systems. They leave you alone if you leave them alone. They’re actually quite small for their heft. That’s kind of their whole gestalt, that they’re actually tiny for their heft.

And, uh, you know, though they’re the darkest phenomenon in the universe, they figure out a way to become the brightest beacons that we see on the edge of what’s observable.

So, they’re, they’re pretty awesome. I also think that they’re fundamental to physics, unlike any other macroscopic object you can think of.

Hmmm. When I think of black holes, I tend to focus on what they do to spacetime. You know, that they cause singularities. It’s their geometry that always grabs me. But that’s not really necessarily the only way to think about black holes. They’re really objects. Real players.

Yeah. I think after people got over the thrill that they actually existed out there and that they could indirectly be detected, there was a sense that they’re not major players in the universe. “Eh, so there’s some black holes out there.”

Quite to the contrary, I think we’ve come to understand that they sculpt our history and our past, that they have a very regulating and important role in determining the shape and size of galaxies and where there might be habitable regions even. And ultimately, we’re kinda doomed to fall into black holes eventually. So, they’re kind of our past and our future.

But, it might surprise people that we had never actually taken a picture of a black hole. All of our evidence had been indirect until about 10 years ago, and that group worked for well over a decade, for some people up to two decades, to try to capture the first picture of a black hole.

It was a tremendous accomplishment, led by Shep Doeleman, who is our guest. So let me tell you about Shep. Shep is a senior research fellow at Harvard University, the assistant director of Harvard’s Black Hole Initiative, also an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.

And he was the founding director of the Event Horizon Telescope Consortium, which is a network of observatories around the world which gave us the first and only images humanity has ever captured of black holes.

Hmm. This sounds like it’s gonna be a great discussion of science at its best.

Yeah, it’s an epic story. Let’s hear from Shep himself.

Shep, welcome to .

It’s good to be here, Janna.

It’s a pleasure to have you on the show. I’m really curious if you remember not just your way into black holes, but your way into the entire idea of thinking about the universe?

Wow. Well, everybody falls in love with astronomy at some point. I don’t care who you are, you fall in love with astronomy. And whether it’s staring up at the night sky, you know, at summer camp or seeing a meteorite, for me, it was seeing a total solar eclipse. I was 13, 1980. And my parents took me out to the middle of the desert in Oregon and at first we thought we weren’t gonna see totality, the clouds were moving in, and then the clouds just parted and we saw this amazing eclipse. It was just tremendous.

Did you think at that moment, “Well, this is what I’m gonna do for the rest of my life”? Or is it that the memory comes back and we reconstruct the story, you know?

That’s a great question. I think it mostly, it just comes back. Life isn’t linear like that. But I will say the idea that there would be these huge objects that were moving and they could align perfectly and allow you to see what would normally be hidden, like the corona of the sun, was startling to me. I mean, it didn’t have to be that way. Like, the angular diameter of the moon doesn’t have to be the same as the sun so they totally block each other out. But these coincidences sometimes give you a special view into nature.

Yeah. I, I love that there’s just this idea that we’re inspired by the firmament, science’s oldest instrument, and that we all have it in common.

Um, so I really feel we have to make a confession ’cause we’ve known each other a really long time. I feel like we met maybe the first week of graduate school at MIT. I think over a cookie table.

So I remember just you were always trying these crazy ideas in graduate school. You were like a creative curiosity in search of a problem. Tell me a little bit first about how you landed on this idea of pursuing a portrait of a black hole?

Portrait of a black hole, I love that. So I graduated high school pretty early. I was 15 years old. And went to college, and then after that I was pretty burned out, and I saw an advertisement that said, “Go to Antarctica and run all these experiments down there.” And I said, “That’s for me.” I interviewed for the position, and somehow they gave it to this 19-year-old kid. They needed some warm body down there to look after the cosmic ray experiments, the aerophotometry experiments, the electromagnetic experiments, and I got a real taste for doing experimental research in difficult circumstances. I just loved it. And then came back to MIT, where I met you in 1988.

Oh, you didn’t have to say the year, man. That was unnecessary [].

I know, when the Earth was cooling. But, I cast around a bit. I started in the X-ray group there, and then I did a little bit of neuroscience looking at biophysics. And then I was introduced to this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope, and this experiment that we use to image black holes and that immediately drew me in.

Yeah. So we’re gonna talk about this project, but when you were in graduate school, what was the status of black holes scientifically? Were they detected? Did everyone believe that they were real astrophysical phenomena?

There was really a sense that black holes existed or strong evidence for them. And of course, there are two flavors of black holes. There are stellar-mass black holes which form during star death. So when a star goes supernova, it will explode the outer shells off, and then the interior part will collapse and if the star is massive enough, it will turn into a black hole, and that black hole could be tens of solar masses.

But then there are these behemoths, these supermassive black holes that live in the centers of galaxies. And while there can be many stellar-mass black holes in a galaxy, there’s probably just one, maybe two, supermassive black holes at the core of any given galaxy.

And for the stellar-mass black holes, people had seen these X-ray binaries, and they were seeing very fast fluctuations in X-rays and even in the radio from these stellar-sized sources. And everything fit with this idea that there was a black hole eating another star that goes an X-ray binary.

And that was Cygnus X-1, a first X-ray object in the direction of the constellation Cygnus, right?

Exactly, it was those kinds of sources. And then the radio people predominantly had seen some very high-resolution images that were very troubling. So you would see in the optical, a galaxy would look like a normal run-of-the-mill galaxy with a lot of optical light coming from stars.

But then if you looked at it in the radio, you would see these oppositely directed jets of material all tracing to the center of the galaxy. What is causing that?

And the best idea that people had for that was a spinning supermassive black hole that was energizing jets that moved at near light speed from the north and south pole of that black hole, and it was piercing the entire galaxy.

So from two completely different lines of inquiry you had one flavor of black holes being suspected from the X-ray, and you had another suspected predominantly by the radio.

So even though people started to theorize that these must be black holes, nobody had taken a picture of a black hole, not in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, the noughts. I think that was a surprise to people because we talked about them as being such compelling inhabitants of the universe, death states of stars, but we had actually technically never seen one directly. Never taken a portrait. And that’s really what you set out to do in many ways.

Yeah. I think the simplest way of saying it is that seeing is believing in a certain way. I mean, you can theorize something, but actually seeing it confers a reality on things that you don’t get otherwise. And there were some really important signatures, too. It wasn’t just seeing it. It was measuring it. Taking the measure of the thing not only gives you confidence in its reality, but you can test predictions.

So in 1915, when Einstein came with his theory of general relativity, which governs the space time around a black hole, and then the year after that Schwarzschild solved it in the trenches of World War I, a story that we know well, even after that, it was pretty clear that if you went to the conclusion of that solution, you would wind up seeing a ring of light around the black hole.

That if a bunch of gas was drawn to the black hole, it heated up to hundreds of billions of degrees because you’re confining it to a small volume, and it emits light. That light would be curved by the gravitational force of the black hole. And from any direction that you look at the black hole, you would see a ring of light. Basically, the emission from behind the black hole lensed around into a ring. And the size of that ring you can derive from Einstein’s equations.

And so we theorized that if we could make a photo, if we could see this ring, we’d be able to measure the mass of the black hole. But also just the ring itself would be like the best evidence for the existence of supermassive black holes at that scale. So it wasn’t just a coffee table book we were after. We were after the real measurement of the fundamental nature of the universe.

Now, when people hear this idea that you’re gonna try to turn the Earth into a telescope or a telescope the size of the world, it sounds like such a crazy lark. What made you think it was viable? It was no mean feat.

Yeah. Well, so, so this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope had been around for a long time, since the ‘60s. And the key is that the angular resolution of a telescope or the ability to magnify things on the sky, it scales as the wavelength of light you’re observing, lambda, divided by the size of your telescope.

So if you wanna see things that are really small in the sky, you either reduce your wavelength of light or you expand the size of your telescope. So you’ll often see these huge blocks of glass on top of mountaintops. These huge optical dishes, and they’re big for a reason. They collect a lot of light, but also the bigger they are, the smaller the objects they can see.

The better the resolution.

The better the resolution, precisely. And so there are some objects that are so small, and black holes are the smallest objects predicted by Einstein’s theory of gravity, that you need extremely big telescopes, extremely fine angular resolution to see them, and you’ve gotta take this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope to the utmost extremes.

You have to operate it at wavelengths that had never been operated before ’cause you have to really go to smaller and smaller wavelengths to get the angular resolution you need. And that’s what took us 20 years, to push the technique to the absolute limit.

Yeah. So there’s a couple of things. One is a lot of people are surprised to hear that black holes are small. They imagine that they’re enormous. Can you explain that to us? Why they’re actually spatially tiny even though they’re incredibly hefty?

Yeah. Black holes simply put are when you confine enough matter into a small enough volume that the force of gravity runs away and the material undergoes catastrophic gravitational collapse into a point of infinite density. And you’d think, “Okay, that’s pretty tiny,” but what happens is that around that is a membrane called the event horizon, and that’s where the gravitational force is so strong that light can’t escape. So that really defines the region of space that we can observe ourselves.

And then astrophysical black holes are not invisible, because you would think to yourself, “Well, if you can’t see it,” because it’s got this event horizon around it, but they attract gas and dust and everything you can imagine to them, and you’re cramming it all into a very, very small space so it heats up. And so in a paradox of their own gravity, these black holes can shine extremely brightly.

And if you get one that’s at the center of a galaxy that weighs millions or billions of times what our sun does, it can outshine all the combined light of the stars in that galaxy. So you see these very small objects, but they can be extremely bright.

So how did they deduce that that’s a black hole if that wasn’t predicted, if that wasn’t expected?

Yeah, a lot of it was the timescale of the variations because that tells you the scale of what you’re looking at. So typically in astronomy, if you see something that is varying on a certain timescale, you just say, “Well, I think it can move faster than the speed of light.” And so this gives you an idea of how big that object can be.

And for its luminosity, it was very difficult to think that there could be anything bigger than a black hole that was causing these kinds of fluctuations. And then there was the amount of energy coming out was related to it falling into this gravitational well and energy being liberated. That was another clue that people had. So as you say, there were these indirect methods of modeling what we were seeing as black holes, and the black holes fit the best.

For the supermassive black holes, there people could see the energy coming out of these jets, and really the only mechanism that we could think of was magnetic fields twisting in the warped space time of the black hole itself. And like egg beaters twisting around, they fling these charged particles out at near the speed of light. And the observations were so extreme that really that’s the only model that fit. And miraculously, as you got better and better angular resolution, as you trace the jet all the way down to the center, it kept looking like this jet.

It didn’t break this model. You kept seeing this jet getting closer and closer and closer, and there was this mad idea that we had to see what was causing this.

So let’s distinguish death states of stars, which are the kinds of objects that were creating signals like Cygnus X-1. Two star systems born and died together. One becomes a black hole, the other starts to descend. It gets cannibalized. It creates these X-rays, these jets. These supermassive black holes, at the time we were calling them quasi-stellar objects or quasars, right? It was not understood where these supermassive black holes came from or if they were so prevalent, if they had permeated the entire universe. I mean, it was a surprise, wasn’t it, that those quasars were commonplace, that they probably exist in every single galaxy.

Yeah. There’s a lot of different lines of evidence for this. Certainly for the galaxies that are radio loud and where you can do interferometry along the lines of what we did to take the picture of the black hole. There, you wind up seeing these jets of material, and those account for maybe 10% of the galaxies that we see. For the other galaxies, we see these cusps of stellar population that increase dramatically as you get to the center, and so you can postulate that there could be a supermassive black hole there.

And now with better resolution and better telescopes, we’ve seen the statistical velocities of stars very, very close to the center of these galaxies within a couple of light years of these galaxies. And it’s now become clear that all galaxies seem to have these super massive black holes at their cores.

And why some are radio loud, why some emit in the radio waves, why some don’t probably has a lot to do with the direction that you’re looking at them. It also has to do with the evolutionary moment in the lifespan of that galaxy. Some radio loud at some times and some not at other times. So we’re seeing the great variety, like the zoo of galaxies across cosmic time, and we’re fortunate that some of them really exhibit these tremendously illuminating radio structures that we can image with an Earth-sized telescope.

And that’s really what drove the field of radio interferometry. We needed to make a picture that was, let’s say, 10,000 times better than anything that we had made before. And the magic of interferometry is that you can detect radio waves from a black hole, let’s say in Chile, and you can time tag them with an atomic clock so you see all the crests and the troughs of these radio waves as they’re coming in. And you can do the same thing in, let’s say Hawai‘i. And then you can bring those waveforms together and compare them as though they had been received by one huge telescope, and they will be coherent. You can play them back against each other, and you can line up the troughs and the crests. Now this is the secret that allows you to turn the Earth into a telescope.

So this is what you mean when you say very long baseline interferometry or interferometry in general. You’re talking about connecting these dishes around the globe. Now, it’s over decades that this work really begins in imagination, conception, execution. But, when was the Event Horizon Telescope as a project officially founded?

Well, it depends. I’d wrote my thesis in 1995 and pushed the technique up to wavelengths that were close but not quite sufficient to do this black hole imaging. So we had a pretty good idea of where we were going. And then we really started in earnest thinking about it in maybe 1998. And in the middle of a battle there was a total solar eclipse, and apparently both sides put their weapons down and made peace. [] Fearing, fearing the rage of the gods. They thought better of their circumstances.

We need more of those eclipses. Well, this has been a really interesting discussion, and I really appreciate your expertise walking all of us listeners through this topic of black holes. and it really is a very uplifting subject.

Well, It was quite remarkable. I think there’s more ahead.

Looking forward to the next encounter.

items.title: Ask HN: Are you tired too in this AI era?
items.author: mellosty
items.content:
Although AI lets us do much more, I feel considerably more tired than before.

We need to keep track of many things happening in parallel and read enormous amounts of generated text. The constant guardrailing, decision making, and context switching overload me.

I am pretty sure most of you are experiencing the same as me, but: Have you found ways of using AI without increasing mental overload?

I would love to hear your tips, but still be relevant in this AI era, so my boss does not fire me.

items.title: Backdoor in Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace
items.author: _chall
items.content:
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.

Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode or and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.

Update (31 October 2026):Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions and distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only ; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.

Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, and , from its marketplace.

While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.

The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.

Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status instead of returning . Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches , it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.

In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.

The Cursor Marketplace Extension

The compromised file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal and exports, and UI code.

The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (, , , , , and ) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.

Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access

First, the payload makes sure exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to , setting permissions to on the directory and on the file.

The key uses the comment . Before appending, the script checks whether is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

Here, holds the existing contents of , and is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).

With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:

  • tries to enable and start or via , falling back to and .
  • checks Remote Login and, if it reports , tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
  • tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.

None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.

It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function () that hardcodes , which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.

A bug in the macOS SSH logic?

On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against . It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains :

Notice that the second command () uses , while the first command () doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:

refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status . The malware’s helper grabs stdout and returns it:

Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", evaluates to .

As a result, the script skips the block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.

This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.

Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.

Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel

Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to as the user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment .

It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:

  • The public key added to () lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
  • The embedded private key () lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.

The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with , followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:

The tunnel uses for remote port forwarding. Passing asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to on the victim’s machine:

Because the tunnel runs with , it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.

The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, is ignored, and are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (), and is turned on.

If is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard . It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.

Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available

To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:

, Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an entry to the user’s crontab.Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
, , ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plistWrites a user LaunchAgent that runs with and set to , then loads it via .Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
, , %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmdTries to create a scheduled task named running as on startup. If that fails, drops into the user’s Startup folder.Creating a task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.

On macOS and Linux, the script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to before starting the reconnection loop.

On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as inside :

Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:

  • Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
  • Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
  • Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
  • Up to 40 environment variable (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i

The environment variable check uses :

Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.

To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries , falling back to .

It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to on both and :

Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.

The beacon is scheduled once with (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with . It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.

From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.

SSH Key and Configuration Changes

Because the malware appends to directly using Node’s , process-only rules watching for shell commands like or touching won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (, , etc.) creating or writing to .

Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.

While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.

User LaunchAgent Persistence

The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:

  • A non-Apple process writing a plist with a label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
  • A LaunchAgent configured to execute against a hidden script in the user’s home directory ().

Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and later manages directly, the subsequent processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of and back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.

SSH Tunnels and Follow-On Access

On the process and network side, look for:

  • or launched with remote port forwarding () and identity files pulled from or .
  • Outbound SSH connections to on port 22, alongside HTTP POST requests to (and connection attempts to ).

If you find a host where this extension ran, it’s important to check whether the tunnel was merely established or whether an operator actually logged in through it. Because inbound sessions arrive through the local port forward, successful logins in SSH logs will appear to come from ( or ) authenticating with the key.

If you identify an affected machine, uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor. Make sure your response covers all of the stages it drops:

  1. Kill active tunnel processes: Terminate the retry loop and any or processes connecting to .
  2. Unload and delete ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist on macOS (or clean up the cron entry on Linux / scheduled task and Startup script on Windows), and remove and .
  3. Clean up SSH keys and state: Remove the public key from , delete , and verify that Remote Login (SSH) hasn’t been enabled unexpectedly.
  4. If SSH was enabled on the host, or if there’s any evidence of an inbound login, rotate any credentials or tokens that were accessible to that user account (especially those matching the KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP environment variable filter).

Phorion’s out-of-the-box detection coverage flags the macOS persistence used in this attack across multiple rules, including non-Apple processes creating LaunchAgents and LaunchAgents executing shell scripts from hidden directories.

Beyond persistence, Phorion’s file access telemetry captures the IDE extension host modifying directly, and Phorion Protections can be used to lock down so that only authorised processes can read or modify SSH keys and configuration files in the first place.

Sample and Public-Key Fingerprints

Audio has voice isolation, noise reduction, loudness and automatic ducking under speech. Images, video, voiceover, music and sound effects are generated straight onto the timeline. Export an MP4 with no watermark, or hand off to DaVinci Resolve and Premiere Pro as FCPXML. Arsaze also has background removal, motion tracking, Animate Studio motion graphics, a node editor for AI generation, an After Effects panel (beta), a free portfolio page and free in-browser tools. Every tool works by hand on the timeline, and every one is also a tool your AI can call.

items.title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer
items.author: falperc
items.content:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

items.title: A Pig, the State, and War: Porco Rosso (Kurenai No Buta) (2014)
items.author: simonebrunozzi
items.content:
Historically, animated cartoons and movies have been used as ‘propaganda’ in war (Roffat 2011). Some animated films, however, contribute to conveying an anti-war pacifist point of view (Takai 2011). As such, the film (1992) can be categorized as “anti-war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 144). Although Miyazaki has been attracted by seaplanes designed and manufactured during the period between the First World War and the Second World War (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72), this film conveys the important memory of war, especially the interwar era and the post-Cold War world. Indeed, in an interview just before the release of , Miyazaki stated that the film is relevant to the Gulf War, and referred to the Yugoslav Wars as ethnic and nationalistic conflicts (Miyazaki 1996, p. 519; Miyazaki 2002, p. 95). In this context, the film forwards Miyazaki’s anti-war message. This paper examines (), which is based on 15 pages of The Golden Age of the Flying Boat), a comic created by Hayao Miyazaki and released in the animation journal, , No.14-16 in 1990 (Kiridoshi 2008, p. 72). A synopsis of the comic story is literally “typed” at the beginning of , as follows: “This motion picture is set over the Mediterranean Sea in an age when seaplanes ruled the waves. It tells a story of a valiant pig, who fought against flying pirates, for his pride, for his lover, and for his fortune. The name of the hero of our story is Crimson Pig.” Scholarship on this film has focused on issues of “war and peace,” especially in terms of the “non-war” () message (e.g. Okuda 2003). Similarly, Kazami et al (2002), among others, (Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provide some answers to the central question of the film: Why did Porco turn into a pig? The primary reason is that he was traumatized by the war. Building on Kazami et al’s work, this paper attributes the reason that Porco became a pig to the following three aspects: “man, the state and war” (Waltz, 1959). According Kenneth Waltz, theorist of international politics, the causes of war occur on three levels: individual, domestic, and international. Like Waltz, I argue here that Porco became a pig because he hates the following three factors: man (egoism), the state (nationalism) and war (militarism). Accordingly, my analysis of is situated in the framework of peace research and international relations, such as non-killing philosophy, soft power/hard power, and conflict prevention/conflict resolution. In the field of animation studies, animation films by Studio Ghibli have been frequently analyzed as a case study. Ghibli animation films are “often considered as artistic productions, both entertaining and meaningful” (Gan 2009, p. 36). There are a large number of publications on the Studio Ghibli’s films, particularly those directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004), for instance, examined Miyazaki’s works in comparison with the animated cartoons of Osamu Tezuka, the creator of (1963). Miyazaki’s films also have been discussed compared with Disney animation. For instance, Kaori Yoshida (2011) offered a comparative analysis on Disney’s (1995) and Ghibli’s (1997) in terms of national identity. Moreover, some scholars (e.g. Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008) provided comprehensive thematic or structural analyses of Miyazaki’s films. However, earlier studies on Miyazaki animation, or Miyazaki-related animation films, do not necessarily focus on the issue of war and peace. Therefore, this paper offers an analysis of Miyazaki-related animation films in terms of war and peace (Table 1). Although the Miyazaki-related films in Table 1 do not directly deal with war themselves, all of them are related to war and peace to a certain extent. (1968) was released in the middle of the Vietnam War (1965-1975) and some combat scenes of the film represent the war. Miyazaki was involved as an animator in the creation of the film with director Isao Takahata, a friend and colleague. Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind (1984) is a masterpiece, and the film reflects the international politics during the Cold War. The Giant Warrior () that caused an apocalyptic war, or the Seven Days of Fire, functions as a symbol of nuclear weaponry. The confrontation between Pejite and Tolmekia, the two powerful countries in the story can similarly be regarded as reflection of the Cold War bipolar structure (Akimoto 2014a). Laputa: Castle in the Sky (1986) was also created during the middle of the Cold War. The number of nuclear warheads in the world reached its peak in the mid-1980s, and the military technology of the legendary castle, Laputa, also symbolizes nuclear weapons. In this film, the word, “peace” is used only one time by Muska, who tries to conquer the world by taking possession of Laputa’s military technology. Obviously, this is a “political satire” by Miyazaki (Akimoto 2014b). (1988), a fictional film about a Japanese boy and his little sister at the end of the Pacific War (1941-1945), was not directed by Miyazaki but instead by Isao Takahata, another Studio Ghibli director (Akimoto 2014c), but reflects similar anti-war sentiment. In the post-Cold War context, Miyazaki produced (1992) which depicts the interwar period (1919-1939) of the Adriatic Sea in conjunction with the Yugoslavian War (1991). Miyazaki contributed to the creation of (1994) that has a passing reference to the Second World War (1939-1945). (1997) deals with Japanese civil war as well as confrontation between humans and animals. (2004) and the latest film, (2013) are related to the 2003 Iraq War, and the Asia Pacific War (1931-1945) (Akimoto 2014d; Akimoto 2014e). Thus, the films in which Miyazaki or Studio Ghibli is involved can be analyzed from a perspective of peace research (peace studies), an academic field which examines causes of war and conditions for peace. While ethical and legal issues need to be carefully taken into consideration when teaching Japanese animation (McLelland 2013), Studio Ghibli animation films can be useful as educational materials at the university level (Yonemura 2003, p. 10), particularly in the fields of both peace research and peace education. From the perspective of peace research, makes a particularly rich case study, particularly because Miyazaki won the best feature film award in the 1993 Annecy International Animation Film Festival (Annecy.org 2013). Due to the award, which is one of the most internationally prestigious animation film festivals, the film was internationally acclaimed, and Miyazaki characterized as “Walt Disney Nippon” (Christin 1997, p. 184). Most reviews of and scholarship on tend toward general analysis, lacking a specific focus on war and peace (e.g. Animage 1992, 2011; Kazami et al. 2002; Okuda 2003; Kano 2006; Kiridoshi 2008). Moreover, Miyazaki himself has made similar comments on his own work (Miyazaki 1996, 1997, 2013). Yet, none of the earlier studies of the film have investigated them from a perspective of peace research. In order to examine , which conveys a similar anti-war message to () (2013), which narrates Japan’s interwar period and war responsibility (Akimoto 2013a), this paper employs an interdisciplinary approach which combines peace research with animation studies. As an analytical method, this paper combines keyword analysis described above with sequence analysis of character’s lines as well as historical events. The sequence analysis is useful tool to examine timeline sequence (Abbott 1995) and it is applicable to film studies with a particular focus on character’s lines in historical context. Accordingly, the five main characters as well as historical background of this film need to be overviewed in this section. First, the hero of this film is a pig, Porco Rosso who flies in his crimson seaplane, SAVOIA S-21. As a bounty hunter, he cracks down on Aero Viking (Sky Pirates) in the Adriatic Sea after the First World War. He used to be a human (Marco Paggot) and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force, but he decided to leave the army after the war and cursed himself, turning into a pig. As I outline below, Porco was traumatized by his experiences in the war (Animage 2011, p. 35-37). Second, Madam Gina, a childhood friend of Porco and a madam of Hotel Adriano, is one of the two heroines of this film. In the film, it is said that pilots in the Mediterranean Sea tend to fall in love with her and visit Hotel Adriano for her song. She was married to three pilots who were all members of the Flying Club she organized as a child, but all of them died in the Great War, or in a flight accident. Gina is in secret love with Porco and vice versa (ibid, p. 54-57). Third, Fiyo Piccolo, the other heroine, is a 17-year old female mechanic and the granddaughter of Master Piccolo. She repairs Porco’s seaplane and develops an adolescent infatuation with him (ibid, 43-45). Fourth, Donald Curtis, an American pilot and Porco’s rival, is hired by Aero Viking to fight against Porco. He is a competent pilot and has an ambition to first become a Hollywood movie star, and then US President afterwards. Curtis falls in love with Gina at first sight and falls for Fiyo next (ibid, pp. 48-51). Fifth, the Mamma Aiutos, one of the largest Aero Vikings in the Adriatic Sea, steals and kidnaps for a living after the First World War (ibid, p. 63-65). This study examines the five character’s lines in the following historical context as demonstrated by Table 2 below. At a macro level, the chronology of the interwar period as the historical background for the film needs to be taken into consideration, as this background is crucial in understanding the content of this film. At a micro level, key scenes and main characters’ lines of the film will be examined. This is also imperative to comprehend the implications of the film for the issue of war and peace. The sequence of the nine most significant scenes in the film are as follows: 1) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos 2) Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention” 3) Gina’s Life in War and Peace 4) Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War 5) Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane 6) The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” 7) Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” 8) The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? 9) Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle The main characters’ dialogue in these nine sections accordingly constitute the primary source to be carefully investigated, in combination with my earlier argument, and relevant publications as secondary source in the context of the interwar period. The sequence analysis of the film and characters’ lines will be examined by using keywords in peace research and international politics.1. Porco’s “Non-Killing” Policy: Battle with the Mamma Aiutos The film begins with a scene in which the main character, Porco Rosso (who seems to be enjoying his vacation – drinking wine and taking a nap at a beach), wakes up with a phone call for an emergency. He works as a contract combat fighter pilot in order to crack down on flying pirates and gangs, such as the Mamma Aiutos. Although he left the Italian Army, he works for peace and security of the Adriatic Sea in place of Mussolini’s National Fascist Party. Italy was one of the member states of Security Council on the League of Nations (1920-1946), but its collective security system did not function, and eventually could not prevent the occurrence of the Manchurian Incident (1931) and the Abyssinian Crisis, or the Second Italy-Ethiopian War (1935-1936). In this way, Porco’s work in the film can be seen as police operations, to maintain peace and safety during the time period. As I will discuss, the international system is more anarchic in this age, and the police and military forces of Italy were not necessarily efficient or functional, leading to the populace in the film making a contract with Porco to crack down on flying pirates. In the field of peace research, Glenn D. Paige (2009) examines “non-killing” as an analytical terminology. This paper, therefore, uses the term “non-killing” as a research keyword. In the first battle scene of this film, Porco demonstrates his “non-killing” policy. In order to make money, save hostages, and to keep peace on the Adriatic Sea, Porco decides to crack down on the Mamma Aiutos, but remains true to his “non-killing” principles. In the battle scene with the Mamma Aiutos, it comes to light that Porco has no intention to kill the gang. Instead, he tries to shoot their aircraft without causing serious damage to the pirates and hostages, and then demands that they should leave half the money and hostages in exchange for their lives. Although he calls a bluff saying: “Or I’ll kill all of you,” his policy is very clear early on in the film.Gina’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Prevention”Female characters in this film (Gina and Fiyo) were depicted as attractive and peaceful heroines. In terms of gender studies, Kuwabara (2007) sheds light on the concept of “feminism” and the meaning of the crimson color reflected in the movie. In an application of politics and international relations, Tomoko Shimizu (2004) analyzes Ghibli animation in terms of “soft power” in the post-Cold War era. The concept of “soft power” was proposed by Joseph Nye, a Harvard Professor and political scientist. As opposed to “hard power” which based on military power, “soft power” can be defined as “the ability to get what you want through attraction rather than coercion or payments. It arises from the attractiveness of a country’s culture, political ideas, and policies” (Nye 2004, p. x). In this framework, Japanese animation can be understood as Japanese “soft power,” which works to enhance Japan’s international image and attractiveness as national interest. For example, Nobuyuki Tsugata (2004) used the term “power of Japan animation” to contextualize the Japanese animation industry, which has lasted more than 85 years. Likewise, William Armour (2011) described Japanese animation and manga for learning Japanese language as “soft power pedagogy” (p. 125). In this fashion, Gina and Fiyo, as the two main female characters, become exemplary of the concept of “soft power.” After the battle, Porco drops in the Hotel Adriano run by Madam Gina, a childhood friend. In the film, it is stressed that Gina’s charismatic beauty and elegance prevents violent conflict by air pirates from occurring around her hotel. For instance, Donald Curtis, an American air fighter as a rival of Porco, says: “She is quite a woman… Air pirates and bounty hunters alike leave their quarrels outside.” The reason why the flying gang never fights near the Hotel Adriano can be inferred by the fact that the gang know that Gina lost her husband in WWI, which I will discuss in the next section. When tension builds between Porco and a drunken gang, Gina swiftly intervenes and prevents confrontation from escalating. Gina says to the gang: “Quite a distinguished gathering! You boys must be planning something… Always glad to see you, but no war games here, OK?” One of the gang responses: “We know, Gina. We don’t work within 50 kilometers of here”. Another gang continues: “We’re even polite to the pig!” And then Gina says: “That’s my boys.” This scene reflects Gina’s charm as “soft power” in contrast to gang’s “hard power” results in peaceful conflict resolution. As such, conflict resolution can be divided into the following four phases: 1) preventive diplomacy (conflict prevention), 2) peacemaking (peace enforcement), 3) peacekeeping, and 4) peacebuilding, as proposed by Boutros Ghali, the former UN Secretary General, in his “An Agenda For Peace” (United Nations 1992). In application of the process of conflict resolution, Gina’s approach in the Hotel Adriano can be categorized as “preventive diplomacy” (conflict prevention) by her soft power.Gina’s Life in War and Peace In opposition to her otherwise peaceful and graceful characteristics, Gina’s life seems to be swayed by the time period, especially the war. Gina literally hates war (Isaka 2001, p. 156). The film implies that Gina lost her first husband because of the First World War. The war was triggered by the assassination of Franz Ferdinand of Australia, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. About one month later, Austria-Hungary as an ally of Germany declared a war on Serbia, a key ally of Russia. The two blocks involved the entire Europe and led to the Great War. Originally, Italy was a part of the Central Powers (Triple Alliance) with Germany and Austria-Hungary, but it eventually joined the Allies (Triple Entente) led by the United Kingdom, France, and Russia. This was how the Italian Air Force had to fight against the Austria-Hungary Force in the Adriatic Sea (Matsuki 2013, p. 46). At the beginning of the First World War, the number of combat planes of the Italian Navy was 15, and that of Austria-Hungary was 22. When Italy declared war against Austria-Hungary on 23 May 1915, Italy possessed only 15 combat airplanes, whereas Austria-Hungary already had about 90 warplanes ready to attack Venice. At the end of the war, the total number of the Italian Navy was as many as 1,630, whereas that of Austria-Hungary was around 650. During the war, Italy lost 121 fighter planes and destroyed 132 Austrian-Hungarian combat planes. The most important base for the Italian Navy was Venice, which was assaulted 42 times and 1,037 bombs were dropped on the city. The number of the combat planes involved in the war in the Adriatic Sea can be shown as Table 3. The death toll of Italian pilots from the battle in the Adriatic Sea can be inferred by the number of the loss, and Gina’s husband could be included. Gina has married two other pilots who were also killed in combat. She tells Porco: “One died in the war, one in the Atlantic, and the third in Asia.” Porco asks: “They found him?” And Gina replies: “I got a call today. They found his remains in Bengal. It’s been three years. I’ve got no more tears left.” To which Porco replies: “The good ones always get killed.” Their conversation indicates that Gina’s husbands died due to flight accidents or fell in the line of duty for the Italian Air Force, which Porco left. This is the reason why Gina hates “war” and, moreover, tries to stop Porco from going to the air fight. Gina’s second husband was likely a similarly capable pilot who possibly met with an accident during the flight for adventure or international seaplane race, such as the so-called “Schneider Trophy. ” The award was named after Jacques Schneider, a French industrial manager, and the races were held from 1913 to 1931 (Table 4). As Table 4 demonstrates, Italian pilots won the Schneider Trophy three times, and six races took place in Italy itself. Given Porco’s flying skill as the “ace” of the Italian Air Force, it is entirely likely that Porco or the other members of the Flying Club organized by Gina might have participated in the Schneider Trophy. According to Pierre Pecastaingts (1996), there were no casualties in the race of the Schneider Trophy, training for the races led to fatal accidents, killing five Italian pilots. Accordingly, it is possible that Gina’s second husband met flight accident in preparation for a contest not unlike the Schneider Trophy. Or they might have died in the flying training or military mission of the Italian Air Force. In either scenario, Gina’s wartime and peacetime experiences have been influenced by airplanes, and contributes to her fears for Porco.Porco’s Antipathy towards the State and War Although Porco “fights” for bounty money as a seaplane pilot, he demonstrates antipathy towards the state (nationalism/fascism) and militarism (war). After he left the Hotel Adriano, he goes to a bank. A military parade full of national flags on tanks with a militaristic music took place on the street beside the bank. When Porco enters the bank to withdraw some money, a bank clerk mentions that it “must be nice to make that much money… How about making a contribution to the people with a Patriot Bond?” To which Porco replies, “I’m not a person.” The “patriot bond” is meant to be a war bond, necessary to prepare and wage wars by the Italian government. Here, Porco clearly opposes financial contribution to fascism and militarism. Also, this scene reminds Japanese audience of Japan’s response to the 1990 Gulf Crisis, during which, the Japanese government was reluctant to making financial contributions to the US-led multinational forces (Akimoto 2013b). After he leaves the bank, Porco walks down to buy weapons for his seaplane. In accordance with his non-killing policy, Porco purchases only light weapons, so a young weapon trader asks Porco to buy more strong weapons saying: “Just regular bullets? Not high-explosives, or armor-piercing?” Yet, Porco turns him down, replying: “Listen, kid. We’re not fighting a war out there. See you.” Immediately thereafter, the young trader asks his boss: “Hey. Boss… How is war different from bounty hunting?” And the boss sarcastically replies that: “War profiteers are villains. Bounty hunters are just stupid.” These scenes regarding “war bond” and “military weapons” foreground Porco’s hatred towards nationalism (fascism) and militarism, and works to highlight Miyazaki’s own anti-war pacifism and his viewpoint on the 1990 Gulf Crisis and the 1991 Gulf War.Fiyo and Repair of Porco’s Fighter Plane When Porco flies to go to have his seaplane fixed at the Piccolo’s, Curtis, an American seaplane pilot hired by the Mamma Aiutos suddenly attacks Porco. Yet, Porco tries to avoid one-on-one fight mainly because of the engine trouble, but fundamentally due to his non-killing policy. This is how Curtis succeeds in damaging Porco’s seaplane and it leads to a major repair at the Piccolo’s. Fiyo, Piccolo’s granddaughter, designs and plans the repair and rebuilding of Porco’s seaplane. That only female workers who are related to Piccolo are involved in the creation of the new plane is suggestive of the effects of the Great Depression, wherein men travelled for work outside the town or to join the military.The Pig and the Italian Air Force: “Better a Pig than a Fascist” Porco’s anti-fascist attitude is reflected by the fact that also makes reference to (1942), an American romantic drama, which portrays the fight against the Nazis during the Second World War as “war propaganda” (Okuda 2003, p. 137-144). Similarities between the two films include characters, but the purpose of is considered to justify US participation in the war in Europe (ibid, p. 140), whereas that of is oppose killing and war in general. In this regard, its fundamental political message of the film is not only anti-fascism, but also anti-war pacifism. When Porco watches a movie at a theatre, Ferrarin, Porco’s old friend in the Italian Air Force, warns that there are warrants out on Porco for “treason, illegal entry… decadence, pornography and being a lazy pig.” Ferrarin suggests that Porco should come back to the Air Force before the authorities seize his plane. However, Porco flatly declines this offer, saying: “Better a pig than a Fascist.” In response, Ferrarin warns again to “Be careful. They won’t bother with a court of law.” This scene is telling, in that Porco, who used to be a war hero, decided to become and remain a pig because he did not want to be a fascist who supported nationalistic militarism during that time. After their conversation in the theater, as Ferrarin mentioned, Porco and Fiyo are being tailed by the Fascist Secret Police. Fiyo insists that she needs to accompany Porco as a mechanic, but Porco opposed her plan at first. Yet, Fiyo persuaded Porco to come along with him, and Porco finally says: “Take out the right machine gun. I don’t care how small your bottom is. It won’t fit between them.” This implies that in addition to his anti-fascist stance, Porco is also a feminist who respects women, at the sacrifice of weapons on his airplane. When Porco and Fiyo are about to take off, the Fascist Secret Police shoot the plane, and Porco discharges a machine gun at them as warning shots, but does not intend to kill them. These scenes are an additional reflection of Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy, is situated in Miyazaki’s anti-war pacifism.Fiyo’s “Soft Power” and “Peaceful Conflict Resolution” The Mamma Aiutos and other air pirates ambush and take Porco and Fiyo as hostages at Porco’s hideout. When the pirates say they are going to destroy Porco’s fighter plane, Fiyo, as a designer of the plane, strongly objects. She makes an eloquent speech to the boss of the Mamma Aiutos about how brave and proud seaplane pilots are, and how noble and respectful the gang should be. Her attractiveness as Piccolo’s chief plane designer, as well as her peaceful means of conflict resolution, save the plane in addition to Porco’s life. In place of the Mamma Aiutos, Curtis says that he will have a one-on-one battle with Porco. Again, Miyazaki places an emphasis on the soft power of female characters, in brokering peaceful conflict resolution. Where Gina showed her soft power for “conflict prevention” as preventive diplomacy, Fiyo’s courageous approach led to the peaceful and successful ‘conflict resolution’ which prevents confrontation from escalating into violence. This is how Miyazaki makes audience remember the importance of peaceful conflict resolution based on a “non-killing” philosophy.The War and the Spell: Why Did He Turn Into a Pig? The night before the rematch with Curtis, Fiyo asks Porco why he turned into a pic, but he does not directly answer her question. According to Fiyo, her father was in the same unit as a Flight Lieutenant Marco Paggot, or, Porco when he was still human and the ace pilot of the Italian Air Force. Fiyo’s favorite story about the war is that Porco jumped off a cliff to rescue an enemy pilot in a war, which is indicative that Porco was an anti-war humanist long before he became a pig. In the evening, Porco finally tells what happened and implies how he turned into a pig in the last summer of the war. This episode is one of the most important scenes in the film, according to most scholars (Kazami et al. 2002, p. 140; Kano 2006, p. 163; Kiridoshi 2008, p. 79). Porco flew with his old friend Berlini, who had just married two days before the final patrol over the Adriatic. During the flight, they were attacked by Austrian fighter planes. Porco did not have enough leeway to assist Berlini, and turned out to be the only survivor of the battle. Porco was so exhausted and traumatized that he hallucinated and saw other dead pilots going up to the cemetery of fighter planes. Berlini was one of Gina’s husbands, and Porco was the best man at their wedding. The film implies that Porco could not forgive himself for forsaking Berlini and this is one of the main reasons why he decided to cast a spell to turn himself into a pig. It is also understandable that he came to hate humans, the government, and the war that killed his most of his friends and cursed his life. Through his experience, he actually saw that war makes people ugly, egoistic and inhumane. In short, the war, on the basis of egoism, nationalism and militarism, traumatized Porco so much that he decided to turn himself into a pig. Japanese people tend to regard pigs as uglier than any other animal, but ironically, Miyazaki in the film strongly suggests that humans sometimes can be uglier than pigs.Porco’s “Non-Killing” Philosophy in the Final Battle Even in the final battle wagering Fiyo, Porco sticks to his “non-killing” principle and does not attempt to kill Curtis. Indeed, the boss of the Mamma Aiutos offers commentaries that: “The Pig’s not a killer,” and that “The damn fool thinks this isn’t war!” Porco’s strategy is to let Curtis shoot first until he runs out of bullets. Owing to the “barrel roll” flying manoeuver which made Porco “the Ace of the Adriatic,” Porco gets a chance to shoot Curtis’s plane, but he still does not discharge the machine gun. Porco only waits for an opportunity to place a few non-fatal shots into the engine so that he does not need to take Curtis’s life. After Porco and Curtis run out of bullets, they end up in physical altercation. This scene could be considered as animated violence, as Princess Mononoke (Mononoke Hime) (1997) is often criticized as full of “violence and bleeding” (Kusanagi 2003, p. 266-267), but at the same time, it illustrates the foolishness of fighting. At the end, the fight itself turns out to be more of a sport (boxing match) than actual violence or bloodshed. Eventually, Porco wins the boxing match and Gina comes to announce “ceasefire” noting: “Ok, the party is over. The Italian Air Force is coming. Get out of here, everyone.” Again, it is emphasized that Gina, on the basis of her soft power, takes leadership for the ceasefire and prevents the gangs from triggering unnecessary collateral conflicts after the battle. As was the case at the Hotel Adriano, Gina’s role here is conflict prevention based on preventive diplomacy. Thus, Miyazaki stresses the significance of peaceful conflict resolution as “non-killing” through to the end of the film. It has been emphasized and confirmed that Porco became a pig not only because of war (militarism) and the state (nationalism/fascism), or but also because of negative human nature (egoism). This is how he came to detest being a human. In addition, Porco’s “non-killing” philosophy has not changed until the very ending of this film. This film also stresses “soft power” of Gina and Fiyo in the conflict prevention, conflict resolution and ceasefire. In the epilogue of the film, even after the failure of the crackdown by the Italian Air Force, Porco never turns up in front of Fiyo. Instead, Fiyo becomes good friends with Gina as they underwent the subsequent war and turmoil. Curtis became a movie star in the United States and other flying pirates still visit the Hotel Adriano. It is not a gloomy epilogue, but what happened to Porco still remains a mystery. Historically, it is logical to infer that Fiyo and Gina survived the Second World War. Porco’s antipathy towards fascism and war has been consistent throughout this movie, so it is unlikely that Porco would return to the Italian Air Force during the this conflict. However, according to Miyazaki, Porco is supposed to be the fourth husband of Gina (Kano 2006, p. 163) and it is suggested that Porco could be involved in the war not for his country, but for Gina, Fiyo and his friends, and this might be the reason why Porco never shows up in the epilogue narrated by Fiyo. In conclusion, through the comical and romantic animated storyline, this movie conveys Miyazaki’s antiwar pacifism, non-killing philosophy, and the memory of war. items.title: The importance of communities around software
items.author: amcclure
items.content:
I've done a lot of activism for software freedom, over the years. At first it was purely for software freedom and related topics, (such as security, autonomy and privacy) but eventually this has evolved into something more holistic. I believe that the software I use should be held to higher ethical standards than only being free software.

My activism used to focus on strong copyleft licenses, these are licenses which require that the project stay free; that no-one can take the project and make it proprietary. This has taken a backseat, as I now believe that there is something more important than license: . The community around a software project is what dictates the values of the project. A strong copyleft license does still signal that the project cares about software freedom, but, by itself it is not enough.

Copyright has always been a system that upholds the hegemony of the powerful, it enriches corporations at the expense of the working class. Copyleft licenses do use copyright against them, but can only do so much. We are using an abusive system against itself, which is not sustainable or desirable in the long term.

Software being free also states nothing about other ethical values of the project, such as whether it is inclusive and whether it is run by its own community, or by a corporation. It also states nothing about whether the project endorses extractive technologies such as generative models.

As an example of a project which is technically free software, but does not value software freedom at all, consider an AGPL-3.0 project that is dual-licensed under a commercial license and forces a contributor license agreement on its contributors. This project is not community-run at all and is only free software in a narrow sense of the word.

This is why I don't care as much anymore about a project being under a copyleft free software license or a non-copyleft free software license. It is still true that the software being available under a strong copyleft license sends a signal that the project cares about software freedom, but it is not a guarantee.

So, if the license is not the (only) thing we need to look at, what we also need to look at? This depends on your own priorities, of course, but there are a few things I could mention:

  • Does the project have an inclusive code of conduct?
  • Does the code of conduct or contribution policy ban generative models?
  • Is the project completely in the hands of a corporation?
  • Is there a contributor license agreement?
  • Does it endorse proprietary and/or centralized platforms such as Discord and GitHub?
  • What are the values of the lead developers of the project? Do they care about ethics in software?

Try to join the communities of free software projects you use and care about, eventually maybe even try to contribute. Even if you can't code, there are many other tasks that need to be done: community management, documentation, artwork, triage, outreach, and many other tasks. In the end, it's the community around a project that shapes its values, so be a part of that community and push against anything unethical. Speak up, if you can. For every person speaking up, there will be many that can't or won't speak up; be their voice.

Getting together to build software is important. Like stated before, this can mean joining an existing project, but it can also mean creating a new one. It can also mean joining or creating a software cooperative. These are communities of people that develop software together. One community can span multiple projects and we can all help one-another out. Examples include The Starlight Network and Polyphony.
