items.title: LLM Voice
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales ,” or “a round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that be ok, but only as far as an outline. Authors should fill the prose themselves.

Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.

Alessio Ferri, Caer Sanders, Ian Cartwright, Jie Jessie Xia, Joshua Kerievsky, Michael Feathers, Michael Nygard, Scott Davies, and Wei Zhang commented on drafts of this post.

I did not use AI or LLMs in any way while writing this post.

items.title: We're releasing the weights of Mistral Large 4
items.author: kuberwastaken
items.content:
We release the weights of Le Chonk, advancing the frontier of open models in agentic coding and cybersecurity.

Earlier this month, we released Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk), our flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, in public preview. The response to the preview has exceeded our expectations, and we're grateful to our developer community, early-access customers, and partners for their support, collaboration, and feedback.

Since then, we've put that feedback to work while continuing to scale reinforcement learning, driving massive improvements in and defensive . Gains continue to accelerate, with no signs of saturation.

Today, we're releasing the weights of this improved Mistral Large 4. The new model also features substantial gains in reasoning efficiency that give developers greater performance while lowering inference costs.

Mistral Large 4 ranks as the best open-weight model for coding and among the world's most capable open models overall. Trained from scratch on European infrastructure with clear lineage from inception to release, it gives organizations a trusted foundation for Sovereign AI

Mistral is defining the sovereign AI category and leading the open frontier. We're committed to building the world's most capable models and releasing them openly, giving developers, enterprises, and institutions the power to own, customize, and control their AI.

Mistral Large 4 entered public preview with strong results across leading coding benchmarks. Just three weeks of additional reinforcement learning have since propelled it to the forefront of open-weight coding, taking the lead on FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench while matching the best open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with substantially greater token efficiency.

On Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, which assesses end-to-end code quality and whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change, Mistral Large 4 leads with a score of 19.7%.

Pushing the pareto frontier for agentic coding.

Mistral Large 4 delivers frontier coding performance with significantly fewer tokens, making sophisticated coding agents more economical to run at scale.

On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral Large 4 scores 48%, effectively tied with the leading open-weight model, GLM-5.3, while using 47% fewer tokens per task on average.

The gains extend to terminal-based coding workflows. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Mistral Large 4 improved by 13 percentage points to 41% compared to its public preview, taking the lead among open-weight models while reducing output tokens by 30%.

To give developers greater control over this tradeoff between performance and cost, Mistral Large 4 now supports three reasoning modes:

Simple tasks; replaces ‘None’ reasoning mode

Hardest use cases requiring high precision and thorough reasoning

Beyond benchmarks, Mistral Large 4's coding capabilities are validated by human preference. In Surge Code's blind pairwise evaluations, Mistral Large 4 was preferred over leading open-weight models including GLM-5.3, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, ranking behind only Claude Opus 5.5 among the models evaluated.

Since its preview, we've been working with leading cybersecurity vendors to evaluate Mistral Large 4 in real-world environments to test Mistral Large 4’s strengths in vulnerability reproduction and patching.

Mistral Large 4 scores 51% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index, which measures a model’s ability to discover vulnerabilities in a codebase, reproduce and validate them, and patch them without breaking existing functionality. Crucially, Mistral Large 4 handles these legitimate defensive security tasks without unnecessary refusals.

Safety has improved alongside capability. Our model’s built-in guardrails distinguishes between defensive and malicious, offensive cybersecurity tasks. It retains strong performance on Cyber benchmarks, while achieving an average refusal rate of 96.6% on malicious cyber requests, the highest we measure among open models.

Here’s what global leaders in cybersecurity have to say about Mistral Large 4:

In the time since the preview, we carefully monitored cybersecurity-related use in our live traffic. Though we observed the model refusing to comply with black-box attacks against live targets, we see a potential for uplift to conduct real attacks. We are modifying our guardrails accordingly, and will continue updating them in the months to come. 

We are also providing enterprise design partners such as Orange Cyberdefense, with preview access to a specialized variant of Mistral Large 4 optimized for advanced cybersecurity workflows, including penetration testing, vulnerability assessment, and red-teaming. Access is subject to rigorous vetting and contractual safeguards, with testing restricted to owned or explicitly authorized systems in controlled environments.

Meanwhile, customers are tailoring Mistral Large 4 with proprietary security data, policies, detection logic, and threat environments using Mistral . For well-defined cybersecurity tasks, it can be further optimized into smaller, task-specific variants for greater accuracy, making security applications more effective.

Learn more about sovereign AI for cybersecurity and how to work with us.

Mistral Large 4 has continued improving on a range of broad enterprise-use metrics. 

, we improved the model’s ability to perform real-world workflows, especially ones involving the creation and editing of spreadsheets for finance and accounting use cases. This is reflected in our Finch scores climbing to 73.3%, second only to Kimi K3 for open models.

is a critical part of a majority of knowledge work. Our RL pipeline enabled us to reach 84.5% on BrowseComp (starting from an SFT checkpoint that was achieving 75%). This brings Mistral Large 4 at a higher performance than models like GLM-5.3 or DeepSeek Flash 4.1 1017.

Agents deployed by an organization need to be secure. Whether deployed to internal members or external users, agents shouldn’t open you up to threats like system prompt exfiltration or malicious code injection. RL increased our gains on the B3 Agent Security Benchmark, with Mistral Large 4 resisting 97.1% of attacks vs 93.3% in Preview. This places it at the top of the OSS frontier, meaning anyone hosting the model can run a safe agent without additional tuning.

This major investment by Mistral AI reinforces the choice La Banque Postale made over a year ago and underscores the relevance of the long-term strategic partnership we are building together: supporting the emergence of an open and sovereign European AI leader. For a public and citizen bank, technological sovereignty is not optional; it is a key prerequisite for maintaining our customers' trust. The introduction of this open model unlocks new opportunities and use cases. By partnering with Mistral AI, our ambition is to combine the best of human expertise and digital technology to deliver an enhanced experience of both customers and employees over the long term.

Zakaria Moursli, Executive Vice President, Operational Performance, Payments and Digital Services, La Banque Postale

Cyber Vulnerability Triage: an agent reads incoming vulnerability reports, investigates the source code and product context, reproduces the flaws in an isolated sandbox, then writes and iterates on a patch until a canary exploit no longer works.

with no human help, Mistral Large 4 builds Orbital Trace, a live 3D map of roughly 19,000 satellites and debris pieces orbiting Earth. It pulls real tracking data, writes the app, uses it in a browser to catch its own bugs and slowdowns, then fixes what an independent reviewer flags until all requirements pass.

Quantum chemistry solver: Mistral Large 4 writes, from scratch, software that calculates where electrons sit in a molecule, and checks its answers against a standard chemistry tool. It then builds a 3D page around it: pick a molecule such as benzene or water, drag a slider to pull it apart, and watch the electrons regroup as the bond breaks.

As organizations build AI around their knowledge and workflows, sovereignty means that they retain control of the models they depend on and the intelligence they create. 

With Mistral Large 4, that control begins with the model itself. Organizations have the ability to inspect, customize, and deploy the model on their own infrastructure. They can use and improve Mistral Large 4 without depending on Mistral to serve it through an API. Mistral Large 4 was developed and trained from scratch in Europe, giving organizations clarity about the origins of the technology they’re building on. 

Control also extends to how AI operates inside an organization. Organizations can customize Mistral Large 4 around their proprietary data with Mistral , and they can build, govern, and improve the resulting agents and applications using Mistral Mistral’s Applied AI experts can work alongside customer teams to build and deploy these tailored systems. Through that work, teams understand the architecture and decisions behind what they’ve built, along with the methods used to train and operate it, so they can run and improve their AI independently.

Sovereignty does not always require self-hosting; sometimes it just requires deployments that meet your control requirements. For organizations that prefer a managed service, Mistral Large 4 is available through Microsoft Foundry, with private deployment options for Azure developers.

Microsoft and Mistral AI share a commitment to expanding customer choice in next-generation AI. As the first cloud provider to bring Mistral Large 4 to customers, Microsoft is making Mistral’s latest open-weight model available through Microsoft Foundry, an enterprise AI platform built for evaluating, deploying, and operating models at scale. For organizations advancing sovereign AI strategies, this combination offers greater flexibility and control across their data, infrastructure, and AI operations.

Tina Schuchman, Corporate Vice President, Foundry, Microsoft

Start building with Le Chonk

Mistral Large 4 is available to try, deploy, and customize today.

Get started in , through the Mistral , or on . For full control, download the open weights from and deploy on your own infrastructure with vLLM or SGLang. The and have everything you need to get started — and for those who want to go deeper, a full technical report is coming soon.

You can also try the new model in ; give it a feature to build or a bug to fix in your own repository.

Mistral Large 4, is also available through , as an optimized for serving with vLLM. Developers can use the open source for customization or the open source library for high-throughput serving.

Enterprises can also tailor Mistral Large 4 to their proprietary data, use cases, and guardrails with Mistral Forge. to learn more.

The model is available to use under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight licensea modified MIT license. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune, and commercialize, with a single condition: businesses that operate a Model-as-a-Service offering must obtain a separate commercial license from Mistral before using the model commercially.

Starting today, Mistral Large 4 is priced at / M, / M, and / M tokens.

We encourage the community to put Mistral Large 4 to the test. Run your own evaluations, push its limits, and share your findings with us on , , or .

Mistral Large 4 will serve as the foundation for a new generation of specialized and optimized Mistral models. Building on recent releases such as and , we'll continue expanding the frontier of open-weight AI, continuing to give developers and enterprises greater freedom to build, customize, and own their intelligence.

items.title: Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5
items.author: theHocineSaad
items.content:
See model page

Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon is the new #1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, and second only to Claude Opus 5.5 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index

Gemini 4 Carbon scores 59 on Intelligence Index v5, driven by leading performance in complex reasoning, knowledge, and scientific tasks. It also has large gains in coding and knowledge work, particularly when compared to other Gemini models, but it is not leading in all these areas.

As with launch of Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 4 Carbon is being rolled out to selected users and is not yet publicly available. Google is offering a 50% launch discount, with no confirmed end date. All our charts and figures use standard pricing for both Gemini 4 Carbon and Argon.

Key results for Gemini 4 Carbon with high reasoning:

➤ Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index v5, with the #1 score in 4 of the 9 Index evaluations: HLE-Diamond, Terminal-Bench-Science, AA-Omniscience, AutomationBench-AA. Carbon makes substantial gains elsewhere but is not leading in coding and knowledge work

➤ Behind only Claude Opus 5.5 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 59 only 3 points behind Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 62) on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index. Carbon ranks second on both Terminal-Bench 4.0 (64%) and FrontierCode v1.1 (51%), behind Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 56%. Google has historically underperformed in this area and so this improvement stands out.

➤ Improved agentic knowledge work, but not yet leading: On AA-Briefcase, Gemini 4 Carbon (high) scores 1609 Elo, a 126-point improvement over Gemini 4 Argon (high, 1483), but still behind models including Grok 4.7 (xhigh, 1638), Muse Wonder (max, 1659) and Kimi K3.1 Pro (1678). The largest gain comes from Presentation, up 293 Elo to 1598, alongside a 120-point improvement in Analytical Quality to 1671

➤ Lower Cost per Task than Claude Opus 5.5 for comparable overall intelligence: With standard pricing, Gemini 4 Carbon costs $7.76 per Intelligence Index task, ~23% less than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, $10.04) but ~1.2x GPT-6 Astra (max, $6.25). It uses 123k output tokens per task, 29% fewer than Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 173k). At the same $4/$20 standard pricing, its Cost per Task is in line with Gemini 4 Argon ($7.68), while scoring 9 points higher on the Intelligence Index

➤ Leading AA-Omniscience v1.1 score, with low hallucination: Gemini 4 Carbon scores 54 on our recently updated AA-Omniscience v1.1, 6 points ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 48) and 8 points ahead of Gemini 4 Argon (46). Accuracy (% correct) rises 10 points over Argon to 58%, while its hallucination rate rises from 4% to 11%. This is still the second lowest of any model, behind only Argon, compared with 50% for both Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and GPT-6 Astra (max)

items.title: DoorDash to acquire Instacart
items.author: WalterSobchak
items.content:
• Transaction values Instacart at $65.00 per share, representing a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026

  • Together, DoorDash and Instacart would help stores of every size reach more customers with the kinds of innovative technology that the biggest online retailers and grocers build for themselves

  • Consumers to benefit from more choice and access to affordable delivery and savings

  • Dashers and Shoppers to have more earnings opportunities and more choice over when and how they earn

DoorDash, Inc. (NASDAQ: DASH) and Maplebear Inc. (d.b.a. Instacart, NASDAQ: CART) today announced a definitive agreement under which DoorDash will acquire Instacart for a total value of $65.00 for each Instacart share, or an equity value of approximately $17 billion. The aggregate transaction consideration will be at least 75% cash, with Instacart stockholders able to elect cash, DoorDash stock, or a combination of both, subject to proration so that DoorDash stock does not exceed 25% of the aggregate consideration. Instacart's board of directors has unanimously approved the agreement.

DoorDash and Instacart share a mission to help local businesses succeed. Families turn to Instacart for the big weekly shop and to DoorDash for meals and nearly anything else they need from their neighborhood in under an hour. The combined company will offer grocers and retailers of every size DoorDash's delivery network and Instacart's grocery and fulfillment technology, in both apps and on stores' own websites, along with the advertising and AI tools each company has built. On either app, customers pick a store in their own community, and the store makes the sale. Consumers will have more stores to choose from, more savings opportunities when they choose to shop with a local business, and faster delivery options, while Dashers and Shoppers will have more ways to earn.

Most grocery shopping still happens in stores, but more people are buying groceries and everyday goods online. They expect fast, affordable delivery and an easy way to order. The biggest online retailers and grocers are racing ahead, building their own delivery fleets, warehouses, membership programs, and AI shopping assistants. A grocer or retailer running on thin margins cannot build all of that alone, and with AI, the playing field risks being tilted even further away from local commerce.

DoorDash and Instacart believe that communities benefit when Main Street competes, and they build the tools that empower local businesses. Together, they could help local stores grow online. More grocers could deploy Instacart's technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, bringing them more sales and advertising revenue. Brands would gain a scaled alternative for reaching customers online. Grocers could add capacity for online orders through DoorDash's DashMart Fulfillment Services and offer faster, more accurate, and more affordable delivery.

“Grocery is one of the hardest things to get right online. Someone has to pick a ripe avocado, find a substitute you’d choose yourself, and get the ice cream to you before it melts,” said Tony Xu, co-founder and CEO of DoorDash. “Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day. Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery. It’s still early innings, but we know that when more people shop local, more dollars stay local.”

“Over the last 14 years, Instacart has transformed online grocery by helping retailers of all sizes compete and grow, and joining forces with DoorDash allows us to do even more,” said Chris Rogers, CEO of Instacart. “When our purpose-built grocery technology and trusted retailer and brand relationships are combined with DoorDash’s global consumer reach and logistics capabilities, we can create new opportunities for our retail and brand partners, offer an even better experience for customers and shoppers, and deliver compelling value for our shareholders. Together, we can accelerate innovation across the grocery industry and make online grocery more seamless and affordable for the millions of households we serve.”

DoorDash expects many benefits will flow from the transaction, including:

  • More Choice for Consumers: Instacart customers could shop at more than 50,000 additional stores, on top of the nearly 100,000 stores on the Instacart platform today.

  • Two Memberships for the Price of One: DashPass and Instacart+ members would pay one membership fee instead of two, which would save them an estimated $100 million per year on membership fees alone.

  • More Ways to Earn for Dashers and Shoppers: More orders for local businesses can create more earning opportunities, with more choice over when and how they earn, whether that’s grocery orders on a quiet day, restaurant orders at peak times, or both.

DoorDash is proud to share a few of the post-close commitments it is making today that demonstrate how this deal benefits local communities:

  • Open Platform, No Grocery Exclusivity: Local grocers can work with any delivery platform they choose to help them grow.

  • Shoppers Keep What They Love: Instacart Shoppers can keep the features they love, including the flexibility to choose how much they work and the information they need to decide which batches to accept, and choose whether to take on DoorDash orders or keep shopping only on Instacart.

Following closing, DoorDash is expected to keep Instacart’s brand, enterprise technology products, and app. Until the transaction closes, DoorDash and Instacart will continue to operate as separate and independent companies.

The value of $65.00 per Instacart share represents a 26% premium to Instacart's closing price on October 22, 2026, the last trading day before media reports about a possible transaction. Instacart stockholders will have the right to elect to receive, for each Instacart share: (i) $65.00 in cash, (ii) 0.3372 shares of DoorDash common stock, or (iii) a mix of $48.75 in cash and 0.0843 shares of DoorDash common stock, in each case, subject to a cap on the total stock consideration issuable by DoorDash equal to 25% of the aggregate consideration and certain proration mechanics. If stock consideration is oversubscribed, applicable Instacart stockholders will receive stock consideration on a prorated basis.

DoorDash expects to fund the cash portion of the consideration with cash on hand and proceeds from debt financing. DoorDash has entered into a financing commitment letter with JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. providing for a 364-day senior unsecured bridge loan facility in support of the debt component of the transaction, subject to satisfaction or waiver of certain customary conditions. The transaction is not subject to a financing condition. DoorDash is targeting a capital structure that will maintain investment-grade ratings.

The transaction is expected to close in the end of 2027 or the first half of 2028, subject to approval by Instacart stockholders, the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, other regulatory approvals, including in Canada and Israel, and other customary closing conditions. Stockholders holding about 19% of Instacart's outstanding shares have agreed to vote in favor of the transaction.

DoorDash will separately report its third quarter 2026 results today and will discuss the transaction on its earnings call at 5:30 a.m. PT (8:30 a.m. ET). The webcast and transaction materials are available at ir.doordash.com.

Centerview Partners LLC is acting as lead financial advisor to DoorDash, and J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is also acting as a financial advisor to DoorDash. Latham & Watkins LLP is serving as legal counsel to DoorDash. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. acted as sole lead arranger and bookrunner on the committed bridge financing. Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC is acting as financial advisor to Instacart, and Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP and Cooley LLP are serving as legal counsel to Instacart.

DoorDash is building the future of local commerce by connecting people to the best of their neighborhoods. items.title: Hackers expose the identities of more than 40k DHS employees
items.author: firefax
items.content:
A hacking group cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files, exposing the names, phone numbers and addresses of more than 40,000 DHS agents, operatives, and associates, on Wednesday, including those involved in undercover operations.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat.' This is what happens to ICE when you do that," a spokesperson for the hacktivist group behind the breach, the Department of Peace, said in an online statement.

The hackers said they stole the data by subverting DHS's single sign on system, according to an online post. It said it distributed that material to the group Distributed Denial of Secrets, which posted it online in a database called Icepick. The Department of Peace also shared the trove of data with Ryan Ottignon, a U.S.-based journalist, and a Swiss activist known as maia arson crimew. Together, the two created a searchable online database, with crimew doing all of the technical work, Ottignon told NPR.

DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity," because it makes explicit connections between "officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations …along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."

Other activists say the information will be a boon to those investigating DHS and filing freedom of information requests, which, due to a lack of specific information, like names, email addresses, can often yield useless results.

In a statement, DHS said it was "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." The department added that it is taking necessary steps to "ensure all are properly protected."

More than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Another 10,000 relate to Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and its Homeland Security Investigations unit.

Ottignon, who has worked on similar data leak projects in the past, rejected suggestions that he and others connected to the Department of Peace or Distribution Denials of Secrets were doxing government employees.

"We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around into cities and states and all around the country, and they seek to hide who they are. Very frequently using masks, wearing plain clothes. And they do universally unspeakable things to these communities," Ottignon said. He added that he believed that kind of behavior is unacceptable in a free society.

"We need oversight for useful government, if it exists at all. So this is just one step in that oversight process," he added.

In a note attached to the files, the Department of Peace wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs."

Hackers have exposed the identities of tens of thousands of Department of Homeland Security employees. That includes their names, email addresses and phone numbers. NPR immigration correspondent Vanessa Romo is covering this and joins me now. Good morning, Vanessa.

VANESSA ROMO, BYLINE: Good morning, Leila.

FADEL: So tell us about the scope of this breach.

ROMO: Well, this is a massive breach of intelligence for the government. So there is a lot of information out there. The stolen data set includes contact information for more than 41,000 DHS agents, operatives and associates, including those involved in undercover operations. And of those, more than 21,000 records identify employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Another 10,000 unmask the identities of Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and people in Homeland Security Investigations units. And about 1,000 show people who work for the cybersecurity defense agency. That and all - a ton more are available in a searchable database. But the really interesting thing about the way the online tool works is that every personnel file includes the names of supervisors and direct reports. So you can actually follow the chain of command, which we haven't been able to see before in such an explicit way.

FADEL: A lot of information there. How did the hackers get ahold of it?

ROMO: A group of hacktivists calling themselves the Department of Peace said that they obtained the data by subverting DHS' single sign-on system. They then handed all of that raw data over to a group called Distributed Denial of Secrets - or DDoS - which partnered with a Swiss activist who goes by maia arson crimew. And that's who actually created the searchable website that's now available to the public.

FADEL: And did they say - these hackers say why they did this?

ROMO: In a note that was attached to the data, the Department of Peace basically said that it was to level the playing field. They said, quote, "they have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs." Meanwhile, DDoS and other activists involved said that they did it as a public service so that anyone who was investigating the department can file more complete freedom of information requests.

FADEL: What about the argument that this can put ICE officers and others in danger?

ROMO: I spoke to Ryan Ottignon, a journalist who worked with the Swiss activist, crimew, to build that searchable database. And he pushed back on that idea that this was doxing.

RYAN OTTIGNON: We are in a situation in which a group of public officials go around the country, and they seek to hide who they are, very frequently using masks, and they do universally unspeakable things to these communities.

ROMO: He's referring to ICE shooting and killing Americans and noncitizens.

FADEL: Now, DHS has been aggressive about protecting ICE agents' identities. What has it said about the hack?

ROMO: So in a statement, DHS officials said the department was, quote, "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively." They also said that they're taking necessary steps to ensure that everyone is properly protected. And as you mentioned, the Trump administration has pushed back against people publicly naming ICE agents and has regularly said that those who dox ICE officers will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.

FADEL: That's NPR's Vanessa Romo. Thank you, Vanessa.

A previous version of this story misattributed the quote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs," to the DDoS. It was written by the Department of Peace.

items.title: The US added a record 20.2 GWh of battery storage in just 3 months
items.author: ljf
items.content:
The US battery storage market just posted its biggest quarter ever, adding 20.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of new capacity in Q2 2026.

The record quarter brought total battery storage installations for the first half of 2026 to 30.8 GWh – up 23% year over year – according to the new “US Energy Storage Market Outlook” from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

Utility-scale batteries drove the record

Nearly all the growth came from large grid batteries. Utility-scale projects accounted for about 18 GWh of Q2 installations, supported by seven gigawatt-hour-scale projects – four in Arizona, two in California, and one in Utah.

Arizona alone added a record 6.2 GWh, the strongest quarter ever recorded by a single state. Texas added 3.8 GWh, and California installed another 3.6 GWh. Of the utility-scale capacity installed during the quarter, 44% was paired with solar, while 56% was standalone storage.

That matters because batteries can charge when electricity is abundant and relatively cheap, then send it back to the grid when demand and prices rise. During extreme heat, that stored electricity can help cover the evening hours when solar output drops but air-conditioning demand remains high.

Battery storage supplied more electricity to the US grid during the first eight months of 2026 than it did during all of 2025, according to the report.

“This record growth highlights that storage is a powerful reliability tool that strengthens our energy security, meets rising demand, and puts downward pressure on electricity bills,” said Tim Pawlenty, president and CEO of SEIA.

Storage growth spreads beyond California and Texas

More than 74% of US battery storage capacity installed in Q2 2026 was in states that Donald Trump won in the 2024 presidential election, with Arizona, Texas, and Utah leading.

SEIA also notes that US utility-scale battery capacity grew from 88 GWh to 165 GWh during the first 18 months of the Trump administration. Those figures show when and where the capacity entered service, but the report doesn’t attribute individual project investment decisions to a particular administration.

“Energy storage is no longer just a California and Texas story anymore,” said Shan Tomouk, BESS & Energy Lead at Benchmark Minerals. “We’re seeing strong pipeline growth in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Colorado, and several other states.”

Demand is running ahead of previous expectations, so Benchmark raised its storage forecast through 2030 by 11.5%, to 683 GWh. More than 10% of all US battery storage capacity now operating came online in Q2 alone.

Home batteries have a rough quarter

Residential battery storage saw a much weaker quarter. US homes added 657 megawatt-hours (MWh) of batteries in Q2, down 27% year over year.

The report attributes the decline partly to the removal of the federal 25D residential clean energy tax credit and partly to homeowners rushing installations into 2025 ahead of the incentive change.

Benchmark still sees a long-term case for home batteries as electricity costs rise, net-metering rules change, power outages remain a concern, and utilities expand virtual power plant and demand-response programs. But it forecasts residential installations falling 16% in 2026 after jumping 56% in 2025.

Commercial and industrial storage added approximately 1.8 GWh during Q2. Benchmark expects data centers to be a major source of future demand as developers combine batteries with onsite solar, wind, and, in some cases, natural gas generation to work around grid constraints and manage fast-changing power loads.

US battery manufacturing also expanded during the quarter. Tesla brought its third Megafactory online in Texas, with the capacity to produce 50 GWh of Megapacks annually, and began shipping Megapacks containing domestically manufactured lithium iron phosphate cells.

Benchmark now expects the US to install about 71 GWh of battery storage in 2026 – around 20% more than in 2025 – as utilities and grid operators race to keep up with rising electricity demand.

items.title: Chained PHP2Shell exploit roots 25 servers, including US Government servers
items.author: 882542F3884314B
items.content:
Updated: October 29, 2026.

Since this discovery, the Dream research team has been sharing updates and collaborating on an investigation with Palo Alto Networks, the vendor of the firewall in question. More information is available on the Palo Alto Networks website. Additional details are now included in the post itself.

Custom PHP2Shell Exploit Chained with Kernel LPE to Root Versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Firewalls in the Wild

On October 25, Dream researchers uncovered artifacts of what appeared to be a Chinese AI-assisted campaign that rooted 25 servers, including systems in a US government-affiliated environment. The attacker combined PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege-escalation exploit to compromise exposed systems.

The affected devices run specific versions of Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS.

The exploited surface is the PAN-OS management web server, which also fronts the GlobalProtect portal. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 has independently verified the attacker’s tooling and results, and Palo Alto Networks is releasing fixed PAN-OS versions across the affected branches.

After rooting the firewalls, the attacker launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration.

The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure. For government defenders, vulnerability discovery is just the beginning, after which the real challenge extends from identifying vulnerable systems to understanding and containing the access a compromise makes possible.

The research below was conducted with proactive threat hunting using Dream’s autonomous cyber research product, Hero.

Dream researchers identified a complete attack operation that included a custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain (CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619) paired with the Fragnesia kernel privilege escalation (CVE-2026-46300), target lists, exploitation logs, and approximately 40 custom post-exploitation scripts.

This included artifacts of a campaign that had rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers across the United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a US government-affiliated environment.

The discovered artifacts revealed an operation that began with exploit development in a lab environment and ended with persistent access to a US government organization's internal Active Directory domain.

We also observed some evidence of AI-assisted tooling in the attack infrastructure:

  • Claude Code had been installed
  • An AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan was configured with Chinese LLMs DeepSeek and Kimi
  • API keys for the Chinese reconnaissance platform FOFA were present

While we have no direct evidence that the AI tools were specifically used to write the exploit or the post-exploitation scripts, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across ~40 scripts suggest AI-assisted development. That said, this operation does not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack.

The Exploit: Two Vulnerabilities Chained Into One Request

The attacker developed two separate exploits and chained them together to achieve root access on any internet-facing PAN-OS firewall running a vulnerable build in a single HTTP request without any credentials.

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619) — Remote Code Execution

The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell. It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for PAN-OS.

The vulnerability targets PHP's mechanism on the PAN-OS management web server (appweb). PAN-OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack.

The attack works in four orchestrated stages:

  • A1 — Memory Exhaustion (~383MB): The attacker floods the server with crafted multipart POST requests, each containing massive filenames and session progress data. This pushes PHP's memory allocator to its limits, forcing the system into a predictable memory layout.
  • A second request forges the stale session ID length from A1, forcing an out-of-bounds read. The server's response header carries the leaked pointer value — giving the attacker the base address of in the running process.
  • A2 — Stale Reference Setup (~500MB): Another round of memory pressure initializes a session, leaving as a live , then triggers a second OOM that leaves — creating a stale reference the attacker can forge in B2.
  • The final request forges a PHP HashTable entry in the freed memory region. The forged entry's callback points to (PHP's function), and its data points to a shell command string. When PHP's cleanup handler walks the HashTable, it calls the forged destructor — executing arbitrary commands as the user.

Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300) — Kernel Privilege Escalation

Getting code execution as isn't enough since SELinux confines from modifying system files. In order to complete the root, the attacker chained in a second exploit: a Linux kernel vulnerability in the XFRM ESP-in-TCP subsystem.

Fragnesia uses page-cache writes to overwrite — replacing its authentication rules with (accept all). Because the PAM file is only 774 bytes, the exploit uses a per-byte splicing variant to write it precisely. After the overwrite, succeeds without a password.

Both exploits run in a single B2 HTTP request. The total chain — from unauthenticated HTTPS connection to persistent root webshell — completes in under 15 minutes.

The Lab: Version Profiling at Scale

The exploit is not a single fire-and-forget payload. It requires precise memory offsets that differ between PAN-OS versions — the address of , the address of , HashTable structure sizes, and memory geometry parameters that control the heap layout during each stage.

Among the recovered artifacts, we found 11 JSON version profile files — one for each PAN-OS version that had been tested:

PHP 7.4 — RCE as nobody verified in lab, but full chain not calibrated (base build plus one hotfix variant)
1 calibrated, 8 provisionalOne base profile fully lab-tested; the others inherit its geometry or share offsets with neighboring builds

Each profile contains the exact offsets extracted from the binary of that version — with SHA256 hashes of each library, ELF build IDs, and precise memory geometry parameters (chunk sizes, fill counts, drain counts, spray offsets) tuned through lab testing.

The difference between "calibrated" and "provisional" profiles is notable — calibrated means the attacker tested the exploit against a running VM of that version and confirmed the memory geometry works. Provisional means they calculated offsets from the binary but haven't verified on a live instance.

The Campaign Funnel: From 19,000 Discovered to 25 Exploited

With the exploit ready and profiles for 9 exploitable versions, the attacker launched a targeting campaign that followed a clear funnel:

Stage 1: Global Discovery (19,000 targets)

Using FOFA — a Chinese internet asset search engine similar to Shodan — the attacker identified approximately 19,000 internet-facing PAN-OS firewalls worldwide. These were devices with management interfaces exposed to the internet, discoverable through certificate fingerprints and HTTP response signatures.

Stage 2: Version Fingerprinting (5,000 alive)

A custom version scanner ran with 200 concurrent threads against all 19,000 targets, identifying which devices were actually online and what PAN-OS version they were running. Approximately 5,000 responded with version information.

Stage 3: Geographic and Version Filtering (240 targets)

From the 5,000 alive devices, the attacker filtered to servers located in only United States, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. They then further filtered to versions matching their exploit profiles (the PAN-OS 12.1 and 12.2 branches running PHP 8.0.30). This produced a final target list of 240 firewalls.

Since US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts.

Stage 4: Automated Exploitation (24 rooted)

The 240 targets were fed into an automated batch runner that exploited them five at a time, with an 1800-second (30-minute) timeout per target. For each success, the batch:

  • Ran the full PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain
  • Planted a 103-byte PHP root webshell in a publicly accessible directory on the firewall (/unauth/php/change_password.php)
  • Verified root by executing through the webshell
  • Logged the target's hostname and IP to a success CSV

At this point, 24 firewalls had been successfully rooted.

Stage 5: Triage (2 firewalls prioritized)

For 22 of the 24 rooted firewalls, the attacker did nothing beyond planting the webshell. No persistence, no tunnels, no post-exploitation tools. The servers were effectively , allowing the attacker to return through the webshell at any time.

Two servers seemingly associated with one target progressed beyond this stage. Both appeared to belong to a US government-affiliated environment.

Stage 6: The Pivot (Shifting from Firewall to Domain)

Among the 24 rooted firewalls, two belonged to a US government-affiliated organization. The running configuration extracted from the first firewall revealed an environment with characteristics suggesting government affiliation: CAC (Common Access Card) authentication, a specific naming prefix, and standardized government-style asset naming. The configuration file contained the organization's complete internal network topology: domain controllers, a central firewall management server, a Keycloak SSO server, a GitLab instance, GlobalProtect VPN gateways, and the Active Directory domain.

The first firewall was rooted on Oct 23 at 18:14 UTC during the automated batch. But it crashed shortly after — likely from the ~900MB of exploit traffic — and never came back online. The attacker monitored it with 240 automated probes over two hours, waiting for it to recover. It didn't. The second firewall, whose certificate data definitively linked it to the target organization, had timed out during the original batch.

Recognizing the organization's value from the first firewall's configuration, the attacker created a separate, dedicated campaign and successfully exploited it on Oct 24 at 10:09 UTC.

Within hours, the attacker:

Built a persistent tunnel into the internal network.

An 8-port reverse SSH tunnel connected the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure, forwarding access to:

  • Domain controllers (LDAP, LDAPS, RDP)
  • The internal firewall management server
  • GlobalProtect VPN infrastructure
  • A SOCKS5 proxy for arbitrary internal network access

The tunnel was wrapped in a systemd service and an boot hook, both launching scripts from — it survives reboots and automatically reconnects.

Exploited the management server through the tunnel. At 11:35 UTC, less than 90 minutes after rooting the second firewall, the attacker used the newly gained server access and the same PHP2Shell + Fragnesia chain against a third government server - the internal firewall management server that was only reachable through the tunnel. This server centrally manages all of the organization's firewalls. Compromising it gave the attacker access to every managed firewall's configuration, credentials, and network settings. This brought the total number of servers exploited to 25.

Launched an AD attack campaign from the management server. Because the management server already had LDAP connectivity to Active Directory (it needs it to authenticate VPN users), the attacker used it as their launch platform for domain attacks:

  • Decrypted the LDAP service account password — the device config stores it encrypted, but with root access the attacker has the master key. They extracted it in plaintext and hardcoded it into every subsequent script.
  • Enumerated every user and group in the domain via LDAP queries.
  • Sprayed passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords. The domain had — meaning no account lockout, allowing unlimited spray attempts.
  • Attempted to create backdoor AD accounts — both a user account (tried in every OU) and a machine account (exploiting the default setting).
  • Analyzed AD ACL chains for privilege escalation paths.
  • Attempted SAML signing key extraction from the Keycloak IdP configuration.
  • Probed Keycloak SSO for authentication bypass.

The attack results — whether the password spray found valid credentials, whether the backdoor accounts were created, whether SAML keys were extracted — stayed on the management server's local filesystem and were not among the artifacts we recovered. This means we cannot determine the full extent of the compromise.

Management Server → Active Directory

LDAP password decrypted from config
Full user & group enumeration
Password spray (all users, no lockout)
Backdoor user + machine account creation
SAML signing key extraction

What the Attacker Has Now

From the recovered artifacts, we can confirm the attacker possesses:

  • Persistent remote access to the organization's internal network via a boot-surviving reverse tunnel and SOCKS proxy — likely still active
  • Root webshells on two firewalls and the firewall management server — likely still active
  • The full Active Directory user and group listing — a complete organizational blueprint
  • Decrypted LDAP service account credentials — enabling direct AD queries at any time
  • Private keys harvested from the PAN-OS firewall filesystem — HA replication keys, SSL/TLS certificate keys, and device authentication keys
  • Complete network topology — every IP, hostname, subnet, server role, and VPN gateway
  • SAML IdP configuration with weak security settings (validate-idp-certificate: no)
  • 22 additional parked firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea — ready for exploitation at any time

What we cannot determine is whether the password spray, backdoor account creation, or SAML key extraction succeeded. If any of these attacks worked, the compromise extends far beyond the perimeter firewalls into the organization's identity infrastructure.

We do not attribute this activity to a named threat actor. Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 tracks this activity as CL-UNK-1280 and attributes it to a Chinese-speaking attacker in the UTC+8 time zone. However, multiple indicators point to a Chinese-nexus operation:

US, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea exclusively. These are the primary strategic intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned operations in the Pacific.
The internet reconnaissance platform used to discover targets is a Chinese service.
A Chinese-developed tunneling utility observed among the recovered tools.
The LLMs configured in the aiscan offensive security platform are Chinese language models.
The infrastructure's clock ran on China Standard Time, confirmed by comparing log timestamps against HTTP Date: response headers from targets.
The aiscan session logs contain user messages in Chinese.

This operation demonstrates a level of preparation and capability that sets it apart from opportunistic exploitation. The attacker invested significant effort into vulnerability research — obtaining PAN-OS firmware, decrypting it, extracting PHP libraries, building precise memory profiles for 9 different software versions, and calibrating exploit geometry through lab testing. The exploitation itself was automated and efficient: 240 targets attempted in a single batch, with version-specific profiles selected automatically.

There was a clear-cut focus on government targets.

The attacker scanned 19,000 firewalls, rooted 24, and immediately identified the two that mattered. Within hours of compromising a US government-affiliated firewall, they had tunneled into the internal network, compromised a third server using the same PHP2Shell exploit, and launched a full Active Directory attack campaign — all through a chain that started with a single unauthenticated HTTPS request to a management interface that should never have been exposed to the internet.

The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active webshells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional PAN-OS versions. Palo Alto Networks device telemetry shows continued exploitation attempts against exposed PAN-OS devices.

Closing the Gap Between Discovery and Defense

For governments and critical infrastructure, finding a vulnerability is only the beginning. Defenders need to identify exposed systems, establish what attackers can exploit, and act before a foothold becomes a wider compromise.

Dream addresses that challenge through two complementary cyberdefense platforms:

  • Sphere scales national cyber defense. It maps exposure, prioritizes risks, and detects and responds to attacks across government networks, tailored to each nation’s threats and infrastructure.
  • Hero scales cyber research. Its autonomous research agents help experts investigate threats, discover and validate vulnerabilities—including in software without source code—and develop remediation guidance and patches. This is the tool that was used by Dream researchers to conduct the investigation detailed in this post.

Together, they connect deeper investigation with defense across the national attack surface.

items.title: Zero click, silent, remote Android DoS
items.author: MarkBlah
items.content:
Android Telephony · Zero-Click · Remote DoS

A single malformed SMS crashes on Android, dropping active calls (including emergency calls), with from the victim.

WapPushOverSms
Remote SMS
Android 12–17
5 May 2026
29 Oct 2026
ADB only

An unchecked cast turns a 5-byte header into a negative array size

When Android receives a WAP Push message, WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() reads the WSP header length as a . The value comes back as a , is cast to with no range check, and is then used directly as the size of a new byte array:


    ...

A 5-byte uintvar of decodes to . Cast to a signed 32-bit , that is . Allocating throws an uncaught NegativeArraySizeException on the telephony main thread, killing :

 AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
 AndroidRuntime: Process: com.android.phone
 AndroidRuntime: java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException: -2147483648
 AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:244)
 AndroidRuntime:   at ...WapPushOverSms.dispatchWapPdu(WapPushOverSms.java:339)
 AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler.processMessagePart(InboundSmsHandler.java:1169)
 AndroidRuntime:   at ...InboundSmsHandler$DeliveringState.processMessage(InboundSmsHandler.java:627)

The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user: there is nothing in the inbox, and the victim never sees the sender's number.

The code sits in Android's core telephony framework and has shipped in many releases. The crash has been reproduced from (the reboot loop in issue #2) up to . Google's October 2026 fix was released for , so devices on older versions outside the security-update window, such as Android 12 and 13, run the same code and do not receive the fix.

Remote, silent, and recoverable only with effort

  • The victim does nothing. No tap, no open, no notification.
  • Nothing appears in Messages; the attacker's number is never shown.
  • Calls drop, including emergency calls. Active voice calls terminate with as the process restarts.
  • 1-2 seconds of no service per message while restarts.
  • Carrier redelivery amplifies it. Unacknowledged messages are re-sent by the carrier, re-crashing the phone; a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing.
  • render the device unusable for an extended period.
  • Persistent denial of service. The malformed message stays queued and is retried on every boot, so the phone can crash on startup until it is cleared (recovery below).

Tested across multiple makes and models (Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware, various Samsung Galaxy and A-series) with a 100% reproduction rate.

After hitting the reboot loop on , @sakisdog documented a less destructive recovery (issue #2). The poison messages sit in the pending inbound queue () and are retried on every boot, so Android's reboots the device into recovery roughly every 90 seconds. Deleting just those rows over ADB, in the short window after boot completes, breaks the loop with no factory reset:


adb shell content query --uri content://sms/raw --projection _id:destination_port:date:deleted

adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS allow
adb shell "content delete --uri content://sms/raw --where \"address='<SENDER>'\""
adb shell cmd appops set com.android.shell WRITE_SMS default

adb shell pm clear com.android.providers.telephony

Recovery credited to @sakisdog. It still needs a computer and ADB, and you should choose "wipe data" at the recovery prompt, so for a non-technical user mid-loop it remains out of reach.

This is the distinction the report turns on. It is not a transient crash: it is a remote, zero-click, persistent denial of service that, left untreated, reboots the phone into a recovery prompt every ~90 seconds, driving a normal user to a to recover, which is the exact shape of a "Destructive Remote DoS" in the VRP's published rules.

A remote attacker can cut a phone off from Triple Zero

Dropping calls is not an inconvenience when one of those calls is to emergency services. While a device is under this attack, or stuck in the reboot loop, it cannot reliably place a call to . The attack is remote, needs only the victim's number, and shows them nothing.

Australia treats access to emergency calling as a mandatory property of a mobile service, not a nice-to-have. Under the , administered by the , carriers are required to identify mobile phones that cannot reach Triple Zero, help the customer move to a working device, and stop providing service to the affected handset. Telstra states plainly that it is required to block phones that can no longer call 000, notifying the customer and blocking the device if nothing is done within 28 days.

The consequence is perverse: the regulatory remedy for a phone that can't reach 000 is to , not to patch the OS. So an attacker who can remotely induce that condition on an Android handset can, in effect, get the victim's own device barred from carrier service until it is updated. The regulation exists precisely because loss of emergency-call access is considered a public-safety failure; this bug manufactures that failure on demand.

The framework was tightened in 2024 following the 3G shutdown, which left some phones able to make ordinary calls but unable to reach emergency services, the same functional state this vulnerability produces.

 rawHeaderLen = pduDecoder.getValue32();
 headerLength = () rawHeaderLen;

Google fixed this crash, but not with the bounds check above. On an Android engineer authored commit 735d967, "Fix remote DoS in decodeWapPdu," which shipped in the Android security release for Android 14 through 17. Rather than validate the length, it widens the caught exception so the crash is swallowed, and deletes the triggering message so it cannot re-crash on carrier redelivery or on boot:


- } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException aie) {

This fix is part of the October 2026 Android security update. Devices updated to the October 2026 patch level or later are protected; devices on earlier patch levels remain vulnerable.

The proof-of-concept Android app and full source code are published on GitHub. The app crafts the malformed WAP Push PDU and sends it as a data SMS to a target number.

Warning: this is a working weapon. The repository contains a proof-of-concept that can remotely disrupt and brick mobile phones. It is published strictly for security research, education, and defensive testing.

Only run it against devices you own or are explicitly authorised to test. Using it against anyone else is a crime, and interfering with a person's ability to reach emergency services (000) is a serious criminal offence in Australia and most countries.
